chunks.latin: 43. «Te igitur, clementissime Pater,» usque, «haec sacrosancta sacrificia illibata.» Dirigitur ergo oratio sicut et reliquae orationes juxta regulam fidei, et morem Ecclesiae ad clementissimum Patrem, cujus erga nos peccatores et indignos tanta extitit clementia et misericordia, quantam Apostolus commendat dicens: «Qui etiam proprio Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, quomodo non etiam cum illo omnia nobis donavit» (Rom. VIII, 32). Et iterum: «Deus autem qui dives est in misericordia, propter nimiam charitatem suam qua dilexit nos, cum essemus» «mortui peccatis, convivificavit nos Christo, per hanc gratiam spiritum adoptionis accepimus» (Eph. II, 4), quam commendat Apostolus dicens: «Sed accepistis Spiritum adoptionis filiorum in quo clamanus: Abba, Pater» (Rom. VIII, 15). Et ideo in hoc Spiritu adoptionis, qui postulat pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus, quia eos quos replere dignatur, inenarrabili desiderio gementes et postulantes facit, clamat sacerdos cum Ecclesia non voce, sed corde dicens: «Te igitur, clementissime Pater, supplices rogamus et petimus.» Quae supplicatio et inclinatio cordis ad Deum tantae reverentiae et humilitatis esse debet, ut imitari queat Illud quod de sua supplicatione Apostolus dicit: «Hujus rei gratia flecto genua mea ad Patrem, ex quo omnis paternitas in coelis et in terra nominatur» (Eph. III, 14). In qua flexione genuum non corporis prostratio, sed supplex affectus, et cordis contritio intelligitur. De qua Psalmista ait: «Sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus, cor contritum et humiliatum Deus non despicies» (Ps. L, 19). Secundum hoc ergo dicitur: «Supplices rogamus ac petimus,» et hoc per Jesum Christum Filium tuum Dominum nostrum, per quem omnis supplicatio et petitio nostra ad Deum dirigi debet, tanquam per verum mediatorem et aeternum sacerdotem, qui sedet ad dexteram Patris, et interpellat pro nobis. Pro qua autem re dicit sacerdos ad Deum Patrem «rogamus et petimus,» nisi pro eo quod sequitur, videlicet ut ea quae ipsi offeruntur dona, munera sancta, sacrificia accepta, id est beneplacita habeat et benedicat? Sacerdotum est enim offerre et majestatem Dei invocare; Dei est autem dignanter suscipere, et ea quae offeruntur benedicere, sicut in lege praecipit sacerdotibus dicens: «Sic benedicetis filiis Israel, et dicetis eis,» et post verba benedictionis subjungit: «Invocabunt nomen meum super filios Israel et ego benedicam eis» (Num. VI, 23, 27). Quid apertius? Illi invocabunt et ego benedicam, et tamen supra eis dixerat, sic benedicetis, sed illi exorando, ille largiendo. Ita ergo et in oblatione divini sacrificii sacerdotes exhibent offerendi et supplicandi ministerium; sed Deus largitur benedictionis donum per unum et verum sacerdotem, per quem et oblata sanctificat, et sanctificata acceptat, dicunt itaque.
chunks.english:
“Therefore, most merciful Father,” as far as, “these holy and spotless sacrifices.” So this prayer, like the other prayers, is directed according to the rule of faith and the custom of the Church: it is addressed to the most merciful Father. His mercy and compassion toward us, sinners and unworthy as we are, has been as great as the Apostle praises when he says, “He did not spare even his own Son, but handed him over for us all; how will he not also, along with him, give us everything?” This is in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eight, verse thirty-two.

And again Scripture says, “But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, brought us to life together with Christ; through this grace we have received the spirit of adoption.” This is cited as Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter two, verse four. The Apostle praises that same grace when he says, “But you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: Abba, Father.” This is in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eight, verse fifteen.

Therefore, in this Spirit of adoption, who pleads for us with sighs too deep for words, the priest cries out with the Church—not with his voice, but with his heart—saying, “Therefore, most merciful Father, we humbly pray and beseech.” The Spirit himself makes those whom he deigns to fill sigh and pray with an inexpressible longing.

This humble prayer, this bending of the heart toward God, must be filled with such reverence and humility that it can imitate what the Apostle says about his own prayer: “For this reason I bend my knees to the Father, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.” This is in Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter three, verse fourteen. In that bending of the knees, we should understand not the prostration of the body, but a humble disposition and a contrite heart. About this the Psalmist says, “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.” This is Psalm fifty, verse nineteen.

In this sense, then, the prayer says, “we humbly pray and beseech.” And it does this through Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord. Through him every humble prayer and every request of ours must be directed to God, because he is the true mediator and the eternal priest, who sits at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us.

But for what does the priest say to God the Father, “we pray and beseech”? He says it for what follows: that God would regard as accepted—that is, as pleasing to him—and would bless the gifts, holy offerings, and sacrifices that are offered to him. For it belongs to priests to offer and to call upon the majesty of God. But it belongs to God graciously to receive what is offered and to bless it. This is just as he commands the priests in the Law, saying, “In this way you shall bless the children of Israel, and you shall say to them,” and after the words of blessing he adds, “They shall invoke my name over the children of Israel, and I will bless them.” This is the Book of Numbers, chapter six, verses twenty-three and twenty-seven.

What could be clearer? They will invoke, and I will bless. And yet God had already said to them, “In this way you shall bless.” They bless by pleading; he blesses by giving. So too, in the offering of the divine sacrifice, priests carry out the ministry of offering and supplication. But God gives the gift of blessing through the one true priest: through him he sanctifies what is offered, and through him he accepts what has been sanctified. Therefore they say:
chunks.notes: The printed section number “43” and column markers are editorial and are not voiced in the English. The citation to Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter two, verse four, is spoken as printed, although the quoted wording extends beyond verse four and blends closely with verse five and related Pauline language. The printed “clamanus” has been translated according to the evident sense, “we cry”; the expected reading is “clamamus.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 44. «Uti accepta habeas et benedicas,» ac si suppliter dicant: Petimus ut haec Spiritu tuo sanctifices atque ore tuo benedicas, ut quod nostrae humilitatis geritur ministerio, tuae virtutis impleatur effectu. Quod autem subjungitur: «Haec dona, haec munera, haec sancta sacrificia illibata,» non aliud atque aliud dicitur; sed res una pro sui magnitudine diversa appellatione laudatur, et laudando commendatur. Quae enim divinis offeruntur altaribus et «munera» appellantur, sicut Dominus in Evangelio dicit: «Si offers munus tuum ad altare» (Matth. V, 23), et «dona» vel «sacrificia» dicuntur, sicut ostendit Apostolus dicens: «Omnis namque sacerdos ex hominibus assumptus, pro hominibus constituitur in his quae sunt ad Deum, ut offerat dona et sacrificia pro peccatis» (Hebr. V, I), sed, ut dictum est, ipsa sermonum repetitio tanti sacramenti est commendatio, et piae devotionis excitatio, quia haec sunt vere «sancta» et «illibata,» id est inviolata et incontaminata sacrificia, quae nulla digne possunt verba laudare, quae in mysterio Dominici corporis offeruntur, in cujus figuram hostiae illae veteris legis immaculatae ac sine ullo vitio jubebantur offerri, qualis solus inventus est Christus sine ullo omnino peccato. Sequitur sacerdos et dicit.
chunks.english:
“That you would hold them as accepted and bless them.” It is as though they were humbly saying: We ask you to sanctify these things by your Spirit and bless them by your own word, so that what is carried out through the ministry of our humility may be fulfilled by the power of your strength.

Then the prayer adds, “these gifts, these offerings, these holy and spotless sacrifices.” This does not mean one thing after another, as if they were separate realities. Rather, one single reality is being praised with different names because of its greatness; and by being praised, it is commended.

For the things offered on the divine altars are called “offerings,” as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you are presenting your offering at the altar.” This is the Gospel of Matthew, chapter five, verse twenty-three. They are also called “gifts” or “sacrifices,” as the Apostle shows when he says, “For every priest taken from among human beings is appointed for human beings in the things that pertain to God, so that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.” This is the letter to the Hebrews, chapter five, verse one.

But, as was said, the very repetition of the words is a commendation of so great a sacrament and a stirring up of devout affection. For these are truly “holy” and “spotless”—that is, inviolate and undefiled—sacrifices. No words can praise them worthily. They are offered in the mystery of the Lord’s body. They were prefigured by those victims of the old Law, which had to be offered immaculate and without any defect. Such a victim was found in Christ alone, who was entirely without sin. The priest continues and says:
chunks.notes: The printed section number “44” and column markers are editorial and are not voiced in the English. The printed “suppliter” has been translated according to the evident sense, “humbly”; the expected reading is “suppliciter.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 45. «In primis quae tibi offerimus» usque «famulo tuo papa nostro.» (AUG. in psal. CXXX.) Sic omnino dignum fuit ut inciperet sancta oblatio, videlicet pro Ecclesia Dei sancta catholica toto terrarum orbe diffusa. Ipsa est enim universitas sanguine Domini redempta. Ipsa est haereditas a Patre ei promissa et data, sicut ipse Pater loquitur in psalmo: «Dabo tibi gentes haereditatem» «tuam, et possessionem tuam terminos terrae» (Psal. II, 8). Haec unitas corporis Christi templum Dei est, cui Apostolus dicit: «Templum enim Dei sanctum est quod estis vos» (I Cor. III, 17), omnes qui credunt in Christum, et sic credunt ut diligant. Hoc est enim credere in Christum diligere Christum. Tanquam lapides sunt vivi, de quibus templum Domini aedificatur. Hoc autem templum est ubi rogatur Deus et exaudit. Quisquis enim praeter templum oraverit Deum, non exauditur ad illam pacem supernam, non exauditur ad vitam aeternam, quae non conceditur nisi ei qui in templo Dei orat. Qui orat in pace Ecclesiae, in unitate corporis Christi, quod corpus Christi constat ex multis credentibus in toto orbe terrarum. Et ideo exauditur qui orat in templo, quia ipse orat in spiritu et veritate merito ab ea et pro ea, quia in ea incipit divina oblatio, tanquam dicatur Deo de illa et in illa: «Exaudi nos, Deus, salutaris noster, spes omnium finium terrae et in mari longe» (Psal. LXIV, 6). Ipsa est namque unitas, quae a finibus terrae, id est ab Oriente et Occidente, Septentrione et Meridie ad Dominum clamat, et dicit a finibus terrae: «Ad te clamavi, dum anxiaretur cor meum» (Psal. LX, 3).
chunks.english:
“Which we offer to you in the first place,” as far as, “your servant, our pope.” [Augustine]

It was entirely fitting that the holy offering should begin in this way: namely, for the holy catholic Church of God, spread throughout the whole world. For she is the whole people redeemed by the blood of the Lord. She is the inheritance promised and given to him by the Father, as the Father himself says in the Psalm: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” This is Psalm two, verse eight.

This unity of the body of Christ is the temple of God. To it the Apostle says, “For the temple of God is holy, and you are that temple.” This is Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter three, verse seventeen. This refers to all who believe in Christ, and who believe in such a way that they love. For to believe in Christ means to love Christ. They are like living stones from which the Lord’s temple is built.

This temple is the place where God is prayed to and where he hears. For whoever prays to God outside the temple is not heard for that heavenly peace; he is not heard for eternal life. Eternal life is granted only to the one who prays in the temple of God—that is, the one who prays in the peace of the Church, in the unity of the body of Christ. And that body of Christ is made up of the many believers throughout the whole world.

Therefore, the one who prays in the temple is heard, because he prays in spirit and in truth. Rightly, then, the divine offering begins from the Church and for the Church, and in the Church, as though it were said to God concerning her and within her: “Hear us, O God our Savior, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far away at sea.” This is Psalm sixty-four, verse six.

For she is that unity which cries out to the Lord from the ends of the earth—that is, from east and west, north and south—and says from the ends of the earth, “I cried to you when my heart was in anguish.” This is Psalm sixty, verse three.
chunks.notes: The printed section number “45” and column markers are editorial and are not voiced in the English. Marginal siglum recorded as printed: “(AUG. in psal. CXXX.)”. In the English, per instruction, it is rendered only as “[Augustine].”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 46. (ISID. lib. VIII Origin., c. 1.) Hinc et Ecclesia Graece dicitur, quod in Latinum vertitur convocatio, eo quod omnes ad se convocet, et catholica appellatur, id est universitatis. Non enim, sicut conventicula haereticorum, in aliquibus regionum partibus coarctatur; sed per totum terrarum orbem dilatata diffunditur. Hinc et universitas ab uno cognominata est, eo quod in unitatem colligitur, unde ait Dominus in Evangelio: «Qui mecum non colligit, spargit,» id est qui in unitatem meam non colligitur, a me divisus in dispersionis perditione dissipatur. Pro hac itaque primum in illa oblatione postulatur, ut eam Deus toto orbe terrarum pacificare dignetur, videlicet ne per haereses ac schismata ejus unitas dilanietur, aut adversitate persecutionum ejus tranquillitas perturbetur. Ut enim hanc pacem tam interius quam exterius faciat Deus Ecclesiae suae, et ipse Apostolus orat dicens: «Pax Dei quae exsuperat omnem sensum, custodiat corda vestra et intelligentias vestras in Christo Jesu» (Phil. IV, 7). Et omnem Ecclesiam orare admonet, cum ait: «Volo igitur primo omnium fieri obsecrationes, orationes, postulationes, gratiarum actiones.» Et post paululum: «Ut quietam et tranquillam vitam agamus in omni pietate» (I Tim. II, 1). Postulatur autem omnipotens Deus, ut illam custodire, adunare et regere dignetur. Ipse est enim verus custos populi sui, id est veri Israel, de quo in psalmo cantatur: «Ecce non dormitavit neque dormiet qui custodit Israel» (Ps. CXX, 3). Et iterum: «Nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem, frustra vigilat qui custodit eam» (Psal. CXXVI, 1). Id ipsum autem videtur adunare quod pacificare, id idipsum custodire quod et regere; quia Ecclesiam suam Deus et pacificando adunat, et adunando pacificat, et custodiendo regit, et regendo custodit. Pacificando namque adunat cum omnium fidelium corda in sua pace conjungit, cum omnium fidelium mentes per unitatem fidei, spei et charitatis unius efficit voluntatis, et per Spiritum sanctum charitate diffusa, impleatur in ea quod scriptum est: «Multitudinis credentium autem erat cor unum et anima una» (Act. IV, 32). Et «ecce quam bonum et quam jucundum habitare fratres in unum» (Ps. CXXXI, 1). Custodiendo quoque regit eamdem Ecclesiam, cum inter omnia pericula clementer eam gubernat et dirigit. Cui orantes in psalmo dicimus: «Salvum fac populum tuum, et benedic haereditati tuae, et rege eos et extolle eos usque in aeternum» (Ps. XXVII, 8).
chunks.english:
[Isidore] This is also why the Church is called “Ecclesia” in Greek, a word translated into Latin as “convocation,” because she calls all people together to herself. She is also called “catholic,” meaning “of the whole,” or universal. For she is not confined to some regional corner, as the little gatherings of heretics are. Instead, she is spread abroad and extended throughout the whole world.

For this reason too, “universality” is named from “oneness,” because it is gathered into unity. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whoever does not gather with me scatters.” That is: whoever is not gathered into my unity is separated from me and is dispersed into the ruin of scattering.

Therefore, in that offering, prayer is made first for the Church: that God would graciously give her peace throughout the whole world. That means that her unity may not be torn apart by heresies and schisms, and that her tranquillity may not be disturbed by the hardship of persecutions. The Apostle himself prays that God would give this peace, both inwardly and outwardly, to his Church when he says, “May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” This is Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter four, verse seven.

And he urges the whole Church to pray when he says, “Therefore, I desire first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made.” And a little later he adds, “so that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all godliness.” This is Paul’s first letter to Timothy, chapter two, verse one.

Almighty God is also asked to deign to guard, unite, and govern the Church. For he is the true guardian of his people, that is, of the true Israel. About him the Psalm sings, “Behold, he who guards Israel has not slumbered and will not sleep.” This is Psalm one hundred twenty, verse three. And again, “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain.” This is Psalm one hundred twenty-six, verse one.

Now to unite seems to mean the same thing as to bring peace, and to guard seems to mean the same thing as to govern. For God unites his Church by giving her peace, and gives her peace by uniting her. He governs her by guarding her, and guards her by governing her.

He unites her by giving peace when he joins the hearts of all the faithful in his peace, and when, through the unity of faith, hope, and charity, he makes the minds of all the faithful share one will. Then, through the Holy Spirit, with charity poured out, what is written is fulfilled in her: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul.” This is the Acts of the Apostles, chapter four, verse thirty-two. And again: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.” This is Psalm one hundred thirty-one, verse one.

He also governs that same Church by guarding her, when amid every danger he mercifully guides and directs her. Praying to him in the Psalm, we say, “Save your people, and bless your inheritance; govern them and lift them up forever.” This is Psalm twenty-seven, verse eight.
chunks.notes: The printed section number “46” and column markers are editorial and are not voiced in the English. Marginal siglum recorded as printed: “(ISID. lib. VIII Origin., c. 1.)”. In the English, per instruction, it is rendered only as “[Isidore].” The citation to Paul’s first letter to Timothy, chapter two, verse one, is spoken as printed, though the final quoted clause corresponds to the following verse in the usual division. The printed citation Psalm one hundred thirty-one, verse one is spoken as printed, though the quoted “Behold how good…” is commonly numbered Psalm one hundred thirty-two, verse one in many modern Bibles. The printed citation Psalm twenty-seven, verse eight is spoken as printed; the quoted wording is commonly associated with the following verse in the Vulgate tradition and with Psalm twenty-eight in many modern numberings.  Printed 'id idipsum custodire quod et regere' is an evident misprint for 'et idipsum'; translated by the evident sense ('and to guard seems to mean the same thing as to govern').

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 47. Quod vero post generalem Ecclesiae commendationem adjungitur: «Una cum famulo tuo papa nostro,» ipsa unitas ecclesiastici corporis fortius commendatur, quia divinae religionis cultum, ut beatus Leo scribit, quem in omnes gentes omnesque nationes Dei voluit gratia coruscare, ita Dominus noster Jesus Christus humani generis Salvator instituit, ut hujus muneris sacramentum in beatissimo Petro apostolorum summo principaliter collocaret, atque ab ipso, quasi quodam capite, dona sua vellet in corpus omne manare, ut exsortem se mysterii intelligeret esse divini, qui ausus esset a Petri soliditate recedere. Hunc enim in consortium individuae unitatis assumptum, id quod ipse erat voluit nominari, dicendo: «Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam» (Matth. XV, 18). Unde constat, sicut iterum beatus papa Pelagius docet, ab universi orbis communione separatos esse qui, qualibet dissensione, inter sacra mysteria apostolici pontificis memoriam secundum consuetudinem non frequentant. Sequitur in mysterio:
chunks.english: After the general commemoration of the Church, the prayer adds, “together with your servant, our pope.” By this, the unity of the Church’s body is emphasized even more strongly. For, as blessed Leo writes, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, established the worship of the divine religion—which God’s grace willed to shine among all peoples and all nations—in such a way that he placed the sacrament of this gift chiefly in the most blessed Peter, the chief of the apostles. From Peter, as from a kind of head, Christ willed his gifts to flow into the whole body. Thus anyone who dared to withdraw from Peter’s firmness would understand that he had made himself a stranger to the divine mystery. For Christ took Peter into the fellowship of an undivided unity, and willed that Peter should be called by the very name that Christ himself was, saying, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” This is the Gospel of Matthew, chapter fifteen, verse eighteen. And so it is clear, as blessed Pope Pelagius also teaches, that those who, because of any division whatever, do not customarily mention the apostolic pontiff during the sacred mysteries are separated from the communion of the whole world. The mystery continues:
chunks.notes: The printed citation is “Matth. XV, 18,” spoken as printed. The quoted verse is normally Matthew chapter sixteen, verse eighteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 48. «Et antistite nostro, et omnibus orthodoxis atque apostolicae fidei cultoribus.» Sicut enim universali Ecclesiae commemoratio propter unitatem societatis et pacis conjungitur commemorationi apostolici pontificis, ita dignum et religiosum est ut singulae Ecclesiae commemorationem subjungant suorum antistitum, probantes se per illam orationem dominicae oblationis servare cum eis unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis. Ὀρθόδοξοι autem Graece, Latine «rectae gloriae» dicuntur, eo quod nullo haeretico depravati, rectae fidei confessione Deum glorificent. Iidem ipsi ergo sunt catholicae et apostolicae fidei cultores, catholicae, id est universalis, quam universa ubique servat Ecclesia, ejusdemque et apostolicae, quam in toto mundo apostolorum doctrina fundavit.
chunks.english: “And with our bishop, and with all who are orthodox and who worship according to the apostolic faith.” Just as the commemoration of the universal Church is joined to the commemoration of the apostolic pontiff, for the sake of unity in fellowship and peace, so too it is fitting and religiously right that individual Churches add the commemoration of their own bishops. By that prayer of the Lord’s offering, they show that they keep with their bishops the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. The Greek word orthodoxoi means, in Latin, “people of right glory,” because they have not been corrupted by any heretical teaching, but glorify God by confessing the true faith. These same people, then, are worshipers according to the catholic and apostolic faith: catholic, that is, universal, the faith that the whole Church everywhere preserves; and apostolic as well, because the teaching of the apostles established it throughout the whole world.
chunks.notes: The Greek Ὀρθόδοξοι has been transliterated as orthodoxoi and explained according to Florus’s etymology, “of right glory.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 49. Cultores autem hujus fidei non possunt dici, nisi illi qui quod recte credunt veraciter diligunt. Hoc enim unusquisque colit quod maxime diligit. Unde et de quibusdam gulae et ventris amatoribus ait Apostolus: «quorum Deus venter est» (Phil. III, 19). Ille ergo veritatis cultor, qui jungit fidei dilectionem, ut Deum, de quo recte credit, diligendo colat, et colendo promereatur. Ipsa est fides quam commendat Apostolus dicens: «In Christo enim Jesu neque circumcisio aliquid valet, neque praeputium, sed fides, quae per dilectionem operatur» (Gal. VI, 15).
chunks.english: But people cannot truly be called worshipers according to this faith unless they sincerely love what they rightly believe. For each person worships what he loves most. That is why the Apostle says of certain lovers of gluttony and of the belly, “Their god is their belly.” This is Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter three, verse nineteen. So the worshiper of truth is the person who joins love to faith: by loving God, in whom he rightly believes, he worships him; and by worshiping him, he becomes worthy of reward. This is the faith the Apostle praises when he says, “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.” This is Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter six, verse fifteen.
chunks.notes: The printed citation is “Gal. VI, 15,” spoken as printed. The quoted wording corresponds more closely to Galatians chapter five, verse six; Galatians chapter six, verse fifteen has a similar opening but a different ending.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 50. Completa hac oratione, qua in primis universalis Ecclesia cum apostolico pontifice et omnibus orthodoxis Deo commendatur, adjungitur in conclusione more solito: «Per Christum Dominum nostrum.» Aliter enim nec oratio nec oblatio Ecclesiae Deo offerri potest, nec illa pro quibus Deus exoratur accipere, nisi per unum mediatorem Dei et hominum, qui interpellat pro nobis. Quod ergo offert Ecclesia, offert per illum; quod Deus eamdem Ecclesiam pacificare, custodire, adunare dignetur, praestat per illum: per ipsum nostra ad Deum vota ascendunt, per ipsum divina ad nos dona descendunt. Hoc namque ipse in Evangelio commendat dicens: «Quia ego ad Patrem vado, et quidquid petieritis in nomine meo, hoc faciam, ut clarificetur Pater in Filio» (Joan. XII, 23). Quam petitionis formam in omni oratione sua custodit Ecclesia. Sequitur in mysterio.
chunks.english: When this prayer is completed—the prayer in which, first of all, the universal Church, together with the apostolic pontiff and all the orthodox, is commended to God—the usual conclusion is added: “Through Christ our Lord.” For neither the Church’s prayer nor the Church’s offering can be presented to God in any other way; nor can the Church receive the things for which God is asked, except through the one mediator between God and human beings, who intercedes for us. Therefore, whatever the Church offers, she offers through him. And whatever God graciously grants—that he would pacify, guard, and unite that same Church—he grants through him. Through Christ our prayers rise up to God; through Christ God’s gifts come down to us. For Christ himself teaches this in the Gospel when he says, “Because I am going to the Father, and whatever you ask in my name, I will do this, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.” This is the Gospel of John, chapter twelve, verse twenty-three. The Church preserves this pattern of petition in every one of her prayers. The mystery continues:
chunks.notes: The printed citation is “Joan. XII, 23,” spoken as printed. The wording quoted is closest to John chapter fourteen, verses twelve through thirteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 51. «Memento, Domine, famulorum famularumque tuarum, et omnium circumadstantium, quorum tibi fides cognita est et nota devotio.» In quibus verbis cum primum dicitur: «Memento, Domine, famulorum famularumque tuarum,» et sic deinde subjungitur: «et omnium circumastantium,» manifestum est quod, quasi quidam locus sit, ubi, aliquibus specialiter nominatis, etiam caeterorum qui assistunt in Ecclesia commemoratio adjungatur. In quo itaque loco aut liberum est sacerdoti, quos desideraverit particulariter nominare, et nominatim Deo commendare: aut certe illud ab antiquis observatum est, ut ibi offerentium nomina recitarentur, quod videtur beatus papa Innocentius in quadam epistola significare, ubi ait: «Superfluum est, ut cujus hostiam necdum Deo offeras, ejus ante nomen insinues, quamvis illi incognitum nihil sit. Prius ergo oblationes sunt commendandae, ne tunc eorum nomina, quorum sunt edicenda, ut inter sacra mysteria nominentur, non inter alia quae ante praemittimus, ut ipsi mysteriis viam futuris precibus aperiamus.» Fit ergo haec oratio ad Deum Patrem, ut memor esse dignetur famulorum famularumque suarum, utriusque videlicet sexus sibi servientium, non solum eorum qui nominantur, sed et omnium circumastantium, ac de omnibus et pro omnibus simul dicitur, «quorum tibi fides cognita est et nota devotio,» id est, quam recte credant, quam devote te diligant, tu solus vides in conscientiis singulorum. Tu es enim scrutans corda et renes, et tibi veraciter dictum est: «Tu enim solus nosti corda filiorum hominum,» qui in tuis cultoribus magis oblationem fidei et devotionis requiris; fidei, cum per legislatorem tuum dicis: «Audi, Israel, Dominus Deus tuus Deus unus est» (Deut. VI, 4); devotionis, cum statim adjungit: «Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo» (Ibid., 5). Et hanc [cum] fidem et devotionem Deo offerre, hoc est vere sacrificium salutare, est attendere mandatis. Sequitur in mysterio:
chunks.english: “Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women, and all who stand around, whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is evident to you.” In these words, first it says, “Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women,” and then it adds, “and all who stand around.” This makes clear that there is, as it were, a place in the prayer where certain people may be named individually, and then the commemoration of the others who are present in the Church is added. So at this point, either the priest is free to name particular people whom he wishes and to commend them to God by name, or else the practice observed by the ancients was that the names of those making offerings were recited there. Blessed Pope Innocent seems to indicate this in one of his letters, where he says, “It is unnecessary to mention beforehand the name of a person whose offering you have not yet presented to God, even though nothing is unknown to him. The offerings must first be commended, and only then should the names of those to whom they belong be announced, so that they may be named during the sacred mysteries—not among the other things we say beforehand—so that by the mysteries themselves we may open the way for the prayers that are to follow.” This prayer, then, is directed to God the Father: that he would graciously remember his servants, men and women—that is, people of both sexes who serve him—not only those who are named, but also all who stand around. And about all of them, and for all of them together, it is said, “whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is evident to you.” That is: how rightly they believe, and how devoutly they love you, you alone see in each person’s conscience. For you search hearts and innermost desires, and it is truly said to you, “You alone know the hearts of the children of humankind.” You seek above all, in those who worship you, the offering of faith and devotion: the offering of faith, when you say through your lawgiver, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” This is the book of Deuteronomy, chapter six, verse four. And the offering of devotion, when he immediately adds, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.” This is the book of Deuteronomy, chapter six, verse five. To offer this faith and devotion to God—this is truly a saving sacrifice: it means paying attention to his commandments. The mystery continues:
chunks.notes: The printed Latin has “[cum] fidem,” an editorial insertion; the translation renders the evident sense, “this faith and devotion.” The phrase “Tu enim solus nosti corda filiorum hominum” echoes First Kings chapter eight, verse thirty-nine in the Vulgate tradition, but no citation is printed in the source, so none is added in the translation.  In the Innocent quotation the printed text is corrupt at two places, translated by the evident sense: 'ne tunc eorum nomina … edicenda' is read as 'ac tunc' ('and only then should the names … be announced'), and 'ut ipsi mysteriis' as 'ipsis mysteriis' ('by the mysteries themselves').

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 52. «Qui tibi offerunt hoc sacrificium laudis, tibique reddunt vota sua aeterno Deo vivo et vero.» In quibus verbis considerandum est, quod tota Ecclesia offerat Deo illud sacrificium laudis; et quia de omni multitudine circumstantium fidelium dicitur: «Qui tibi offerunt.» Quod enim adimpletur proprie ministerio sacerdotum, hoc generaliter agitur fide et devotione cunctorum. Omni enim Ecclesiae dicitur per beatum Petrum apostolum: «Vos autem genus electum, regale sacerdotium» (I Petr. II, 9), offerre spiritales hostias et acceptabiles Deo per Jesum Christum. Omnem ergo Ecclesiam sacerdotium sanctum appellat, quod sola domus Aaron in lege nomen et officium habuit, quia nimirum omnes fideles summi sacerdotis membra existunt, cuncti oleo laetitiae signantur, illius corpori uniti, qui rex summus et sacerdos est verus. Regnum suis tribuit ut rex, et ut pontifex eorum peccata sui sanguinis hostia mundans, quanquam et in eadem lege Veteris Testamenti hujus spiritualis sacerdotii, quo tota Ecclesia consecratur, evidenter mysterium commendatur, cum ille agnus in pascha mactandus, quod vobis immolatus est Christus, non a solis sacerdotibus, sed ab universo generaliter populo jubetur immolari, dicente Domino: «Immolabit eum omnis multitudo filiorum Israel ad vesperam» (Exod. XII, 6). Hunc namque agnum in paschali solemnitate immolatum eadem lex et victimam et hostiam et sacrificium esse commendat, praecipiente Domino, et dicente: «Non immolabit super fermento sanguinem hostiae meae, neque residebit mane de victima solemnitatis phase» (Exod. XXXIV, 25). Et iterum: «Nemo,» inquit, «qui fuerit immundus super anima sua, in via procul in gente vestra, faciat phase Domino mense secundo» (Num. IX, 10). Et post pauca: «Si quis autem mundus est, et in itinere non fuit, et tamen non fecit phase, exterminabitur anima illa de populis suis, quia sacrificium Domino non obtulit tempore suo» (Ibid., 13). Offerunt ergo sacerdotes Ecclesiae, offert per ipsos et in ipsis tota Ecclesia Deo sacrificium laudis, quod a cultoribus suis sibi offerri ipse praecepit, dicens: «Immola Deo sacrificium laudis, et redde Altissimo vota tua» (Psal. XLIX, 14).
chunks.english: “They offer to you this sacrifice of praise, and to you they render their vows, to the eternal God, living and true.” In these words we should notice that the whole Church offers that sacrifice of praise to God, because the prayer says of the entire multitude of faithful people standing around, “They offer to you.” What is carried out in the proper sense by the ministry of priests is, in a general sense, done by the faith and devotion of everyone. For blessed Peter the apostle says to the whole Church, “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood.” This is Peter’s first letter, chapter two, verse nine. And he speaks of offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Therefore he calls the whole Church a holy priesthood—a name and office which, under the law, belonged only to the house of Aaron—because all the faithful are members of the high priest. All are signed with the oil of gladness and united to the body of the one who is the highest king and the true priest. As king, Christ gives his own people a kingdom; and as high priest, he cleanses their sins by the sacrifice of his own blood. Yet even in the law of the Old Testament, the mystery of this spiritual priesthood, by which the whole Church is consecrated, is clearly shown. For the lamb to be slaughtered at Passover—which is Christ, sacrificed for you—was commanded to be sacrificed not by the priests alone, but by the whole people in general. The Lord says, “The whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it toward evening.” This is the book of Exodus, chapter twelve, verse six. The same law teaches that this lamb, sacrificed in the solemnity of Passover, is a victim, a sacrificial offering, and a sacrifice, when the Lord commands and says, “You shall not sacrifice the blood of my victim upon leaven, nor shall any of the victim of the solemnity of Passover remain until morning.” This is the book of Exodus, chapter thirty-four, verse twenty-five. And again he says, “Anyone who is unclean in his soul, or far away on a journey among your people, shall keep the Passover to the Lord in the second month.” This is the book of Numbers, chapter nine, verse ten. And a little later: “But if anyone is clean, and was not on a journey, and still did not keep the Passover, that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he did not offer the sacrifice to the Lord at its proper time.” This is the book of Numbers, chapter nine, verse thirteen. Therefore the priests of the Church offer; and through them and in them, the whole Church offers to God the sacrifice of praise—the sacrifice that God himself commanded to be offered to him by those who worship him, saying, “Offer to God the sacrifice of praise, and render your vows to the Most High.” This is Psalm forty-nine, verse fourteen.
chunks.notes: The phrase “offerre spiritales hostias et acceptabiles Deo per Jesum Christum” is printed after the citation to First Peter chapter two, verse nine, but corresponds to First Peter chapter two, verse five; the translation keeps the wording where Florus places it and speaks only the printed citation. “Quod vobis immolatus est Christus” is syntactically awkward in the printed Latin; the translation renders the evident Pauline sense, “which is Christ, sacrificed for you,” echoing First Corinthians chapter five, verse seven, but no citation is printed there.  The printed Latin reads 'Nemo … faciat phase Domino mense secundo' ('No one … shall keep the Passover in the second month'), which reverses Numbers 9:10 (Vulgate 'homo'); the English gives the evident sense, 'Anyone who is unclean … shall keep the Passover to the Lord in the second month.'

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 53. (AUGUSTINUS.) Non quod a nobis tanquam indigens expetat laudem; sed ut in ea nobis consulat ad salutem, sicut et in eodem psalmo iterum dicit: «Sacrificium laudis honorificabit me, et illic via est, ubi ostendam salutare meum» (Ibid., 33). Quid est enim salutare Dei, nisi Filius Dei, Salvator mundi? Ipse igitur sacerdos et victima sacrificium laudis implevit, malorum operum tribuens indulgentiam, et bene operandi largiens gratiam. Ad hoc enim Dominus sacrificium laudis ab ejus cultoribus [Col. 0048D] immolatur, ut qui gloriatur in Domino glorietur. Hoc ergo sacrificium laudis, id est oblationem Dominicae passionis, in qua nulla nostra merita agnoscimus, sed solam Dei gratiam collaudamus; quia in hoc apparuit charitas Dei in nobis, quia unigenitum Filium suum misit Deus in mundum, ut vivamus per eum, non quasi nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos, et misit Filium suum propitiationem pro peccatis nostris. Hanc offert devotio fidelium pro se suisque omnibus, id est ad se vel genere vel familiaritate, vel qualibet alia conditione, sub ejusdem fidei professione pertinentibus, tam viventibus videlicet quam mortuis. Et hoc qua spe fideles [Col. 0049A] faciant subjungitur, quia non pro aliquo terreno appetitu, non pro aliquo temporali lucro, sed solummodo «pro redemptione animarum suarum,» quia, ut Apostolus dicit, «in ipso habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ejus, remissionem peccatorum;» «pro spe salutis et incolumitatis suae,» pro spe videlicet aeternae salutis. Spe enim salvi facti sumus. Si autem quod non videmus speramus, per patientiam exspectamus. Nec solum pro salute aeterna, sed etiam pro temporali incolumitate, id est corporali sanitate. Incolumitas enim sanitatis integritas. Utraque enim salus, animae scilicet et corporis, ab illo est, de quo in psalmo canitur: «Domini est salus.» Et ut utraque ab illo exspectetur, pertinet ad pietatem religionis, de qua testatur Apostolus dicens: «Pietas autem ad omnia utilis est, promissionem vitae habens quae nunc est et futurae.» «Tibi,» inquit, «reddunt vota sua aeterno Deo vivo et vero,» juxta quod in psalmo dicitur: «Et redde Altissimo vota tua,» vota videlicet fidei et piae devotionis, per quam nosmetipsos Deo vovimus et reddimus. Quisquis enim bene cogitat quod Deo voverat et quae vota persolvat, hoc exigitur, hoc debetur, ut seipsum voveat et reddat. Imago Caesaris reddatur Caesari, imago Dei reddatur Deo. [Col. 0049B] Sed sicut videndum est quid offerat, ita etiam considerandum est ubi offerat; quia veri sacrificii extra catholicam Ecclesiam locus non est, unde multum consequenter adjungitur in mysterio.
chunks.english:
[Augustine] God does not ask praise from us because he needs it. Rather, through our praise he provides for our salvation. As the same psalm says again: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show my salvation.” This is cited as Psalm forty-nine, verse thirty-three.

And what is God’s salvation, if not the Son of God, the Savior of the world? He himself, both priest and victim, fulfilled the sacrifice of praise: he grants forgiveness for evil deeds, and gives the grace to do good. The Lord is offered this sacrifice of praise by those who worship him so that whoever boasts may boast in the Lord.

So this sacrifice of praise—that is, the offering of the Lord’s Passion—is the sacrifice in which we recognize no merits of our own, but praise only the grace of God. For in this the love of God appeared among us: God sent his only-begotten Son into the world so that we might live through him. It was not that we loved God first, but that he first loved us and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.

The devotion of the faithful offers this sacrifice for themselves and for all who belong to them: those connected with them by birth, by household relationship, or by any other bond, so long as they share the same profession of faith. This includes both the living and the dead.

The prayer then adds the hope with which the faithful do this. They do not offer for some earthly desire or temporary gain, but only “for the redemption of their souls,” because, as the Apostle says, “in him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins”; and “for the hope of their salvation and well-being”—that is, for the hope of eternal salvation. For we have been saved in hope. And if we hope for what we do not yet see, we wait for it with patience.

But they offer not only for eternal salvation; they also offer for temporal well-being, meaning bodily health. “Well-being” means the wholeness of health. Both kinds of salvation—the salvation of the soul and the health of the body—come from the one of whom the psalm sings, “Salvation belongs to the Lord.” And it belongs to true religious devotion to expect both from him, as the Apostle testifies when he says, “Godliness is useful for all things, holding the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come.”

“They render their vows to you,” he says, “the eternal God, living and true,” in keeping with the psalm’s words: “And render your vows to the Most High.” These are the vows of faith and reverent devotion, by which we vow and render our very selves to God. Anyone who thinks carefully about what he has vowed to God, and what vows he must fulfill, will see that this is what is required and owed: he must vow and render himself. Let Caesar’s image be rendered to Caesar; let God’s image be rendered to God.

But just as we must ask what the faithful offer, we must also consider where they offer it. For there is no place for the true sacrifice outside the catholic Church. For this reason, the mystery very fittingly adds the following words.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “(AUGUSTINUS.)”. The citation “(Ibid., 33)” is rendered as printed. It appears to refer back to Psalm forty-nine from the preceding section, but the quoted verse corresponds to Psalm forty-nine, verse twenty-three in the Vulgate numbering, not verse thirty-three.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 54. «Communicantes et memoriam venerantes, in primis,» etc., usque «et omnium sanctorum tuorum.» (AUG.) Quos dicit communicantes et memoriam venerantes beatae Genitricis Dei, et apostolorum et martyrum, et omnium sanctorum, nisi et seipsum sacerdos qui offert, et omnes circumstantes, qui simul offerunt unum sacrificium laudis? Quod ut Deo possit esse acceptum et beneplacitum, non alibi hoc offerunt et sacerdotes et Ecclesia cum sacerdotibus, nisi in communione et societate sanctorum, in quibus voluit idem omnipotens Deus Ecclesiae [Col. 0049C] suae constare fundamentum, sicut Apostolus dicit: «Estis cives sanctorum et domestici Dei, superaedificati super fundamentum apostolorum et prophetarum» (Eph. II, 19). In eorum ergo communione et memoriae veneratione tanquam in templo vero Dei, offert devotio fidelium Deo vota et munera sua, et ideo fiunt communicantes eorum memoriae tanquam filii patrum et sectatores praecedentium. Quid est enim «communicantes,» nisi «communionem et societatem tenentes?» Et quid est eorum memoriam venerari, nisi cum pietate et humilitate eorum vestigia sequi? Ad hanc societatem nos beatus Joannes apostolus invitans ait: «Quod vidimus et audivimus, annuntiamus vobis.» Et quasi interrogaremus quid nobis prodesset illa annuntiatio, ait: «Ut et vos societatem»[Col. 0049D] «habeatis nobiscum.» Et ne quis contemnendum putaret hanc societatem tanquam hominum, continuo adjunxit: «Et societas nostra sit cum Patre et cum Filio ejus» Jesu Christo, manifeste ostendens, quia quicumque societatem cum Deo habere desiderant, primo Ecclesiae societati debent adunari, illamque fidem addiscere, et ejus sacramentis imbui, quam apostoli ab ipsa praesente in carne Veritate perceperunt. Pro ipsa enim et sancti martyres passi sunt, et ipsa catholica fundatur Ecclesia, cui beatae et gloriosae Virginis partus exstitit salutis exordium.
chunks.english:
“In communion with, and honoring the memory, first of all,” and so on, as far as, “and of all your saints.”

[Augustine] Who are the ones said to be “in communion with” and “honoring the memory” of the blessed Mother of God, and of the apostles, martyrs, and all the saints? They are the priest who offers, and all who stand around him, who together offer one sacrifice of praise.

For this sacrifice to be acceptable and pleasing to God, the priests and the Church together with the priests offer it nowhere except in the communion and fellowship of the saints. In those saints, the same almighty God willed the foundation of his Church to stand firm. As the Apostle says, “You are fellow citizens of the saints and members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets.” This is Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter two, verse nineteen.

Therefore, in communion with them, and in reverent remembrance of them, the devotion of the faithful offers its vows and gifts to God, as if in the true temple of God. In this way the faithful become sharers in their memory, like children of the fathers and followers of those who went before them.

For what does “in communion with” mean, if not “holding communion and fellowship”? And what does it mean to honor their memory, if not to follow their footsteps with reverence and humility?

The blessed apostle John invites us into this fellowship when he says, “What we have seen and heard, we proclaim to you.” And as if we had asked what benefit that proclamation brings us, he says, “so that you also may have fellowship with us.” Then, so that no one would think this fellowship could be despised as merely human, he immediately adds, “And our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son,” Jesus Christ.

By this he clearly shows that all who desire fellowship with God must first be united to the fellowship of the Church. They must learn that faith, and be formed by those sacraments, which the apostles received from Truth itself while he was present in the flesh. For that faith the holy martyrs suffered, and upon it the catholic Church is founded—the Church for whom the childbearing of the blessed and glorious Virgin became the beginning of salvation.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “(AUG.)”. The liturgical lemma is abbreviated in the Latin with “etc.” and “usque”; the translation preserves the abbreviation rather than completing the Canon from memory.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 55. (AUG., serm. 186). Quae vere semper creditur virgo, quia vel si Domino nascente corrumperetur [Col. 0050A] ejus integritas, non jam ille de Virgine nasceretur, cum que falso, quod absit, natum de virgine Maria tota confiteretur Ecclesia, cui pro humani generis salute vero homini facto singulari munere datum est ut, statim ex quo in utero Virginis concipi et homo fieri inciperet, verus esset et Deus: unde et eadem gloriosa semper virgo Maria vere Dei genitrix credenda et confitenda est. Ipsa ergo in hac venerabili commemoratione sanctorum prima ponitur, per quam et illi et nos meruimus auctorem vitae suscipere, et ei conjungitur communicatio beatorum apostolorum et martyrum, non solum qui hic nominatim exprimuntur, sed et omnium quorum nec numerum nec nomina scire possumus. Et tamen, per gratiam fidei et charitatis, si istis paucis et praecipuis nominatis pie adhaeremus, etiam illis quos nosse [Col. 0050B] non possumus, in horum communione copulati sumus, servantes societatem spiritus in vinculo pacis, ut cum eis unum corpus et unus spiritus simus. Sequitur in mysterio:
chunks.english:
[Augustine] She is truly believed to be ever-virgin. For if her bodily integrity had been violated when the Lord was born, then he would no longer have been born of a virgin. In that case, which God forbid, the whole Church would falsely confess that he was born of the Virgin Mary.

For the salvation of the human race, he truly became man. Yet he was granted this unique gift: from the very moment when he began to be conceived in the Virgin’s womb and to become man, he was also true God. Therefore the same glorious ever-virgin Mary must truly be believed and confessed to be the Mother of God.

So she is placed first in this venerable commemoration of the saints, because through her both they and we were found worthy to receive the Author of life. Joined to her is the communion of the blessed apostles and martyrs—not only those who are named here one by one, but all those whose number and names we cannot know.

And yet, by the grace of faith and love, if we devoutly cling to those few and foremost saints who are named, we are joined, in their communion, even to those whom we cannot know. We keep the fellowship of the Spirit in the bond of peace, so that with them we may be one body and one spirit.

The mystery continues:
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “(AUG., serm. 186).” The Latin “Genitrix Dei” and “Dei genitrix” are translated as “Mother of God,” preserving the Christological sense of Theotokos without introducing Greek into the narration.  Printed 'cum que falso' is read as 'cumque falso' (a word-division misprint); translated by the evident sense.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 56. «Quorum meritis precibusque concedas.» Propter merita namque et intercessiones sublimium justorum, quos intercessores et patronos quaerimus, nostrae infirmitati Dominus miseretur et propitiatur, ut in omnibus, sive adversis, sive prosperis, ne vel in istis deficiamus, vel in illis decipiamur, protectionis ejus muniamur auxilio.
chunks.english:
“By whose merits and prayers may you grant.”

For because of the merits and intercessions of those exalted righteous ones—whom we seek as intercessors and patrons—the Lord has mercy on our weakness and is gracious to us. Thus in every circumstance, whether adverse or favorable, we are fortified by the help of his protection: so that in hardships we do not collapse, and in prosperity we are not deceived.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 57. (VIGILIUS.) Denique obsesso ab hostibus Ezechiae et auxilium ejus invocanti ait: «Et civitatem hanc salvabo, et protegam eam propter me, et propter David servum meum» (IV Reg. XXXI, 6); sic et Moyses pro populo peccante intercedens patrum fecit memoriam, et ita deprecans Dominum placare curabat: «Quiescat,» inquiens, «ira tua, et esto placabilis super nequitia populi tui.»[Col. 0050C] «Recordare Abraham, Isaac et Israel servorum tuorum, quibus jurasti per temetipsum dicens: Multiplicabo semen tuum sicut stellas coeli» (Exod. XXXII, 13). Nec dubitandum est fidelium petitiones a spiritibus justorum sciri, quia qui intus omnipotentis Dei claritatem vident, nullo modo credendum est quia sit foris aliquid quod ignorent. Postulat ergo Ecclesia suffragia sanctorum martyrum, nec tamen erigit altaria inquibus sacrificet martyribus, sed uni Deo et martyrum et nostro. (AUG., de Civ. Dei, l. XXII, c. 10.) Ad quod sacrificium sicut homines Dei, qui mundum in ejus confessione vicerunt, suo loco et ordine nominantur, non tamen a sacerdote qui sacrificat invocantur. Deo quippe, non ipsis sacrificat, quamvis in memoriis sacrificet eorum, quia Dei sacerdos est, [Col. 0050D] non illorum. Ipsum vero sacrificium est Christi, quod non offertur ipsis, quia hoc sunt et ipsi. Sequitur in mysterio:
chunks.english:
[Vigilius] Finally, when Hezekiah was besieged by enemies and called upon God’s help, God said to him: “I will save this city and protect it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.” This is cited as the Fourth Book of Kings, chapter thirty-one, verse six.

In the same way, when Moses interceded for the sinful people, he recalled the fathers and tried to appease the Lord by praying: “Let your anger rest,” he said, “and be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by your own self, saying: I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven.” This is the Book of Exodus, chapter thirty-two, verse thirteen.

Nor should we doubt that the requests of the faithful are known to the spirits of the righteous. Those who behold the brightness of almighty God within cannot be thought ignorant of anything outside.

Therefore the Church asks for the support of the holy martyrs. Yet she does not set up altars on which she sacrifices to the martyrs, but to the one God who is both their God and ours.

[Augustine] In that sacrifice, the human beings of God who conquered the world by confessing him are named in their proper place and order. But they are not invoked by the priest who offers the sacrifice. For he sacrifices to God, not to them, even though he sacrifices at their memorials, because he is God’s priest, not theirs. The sacrifice itself is Christ’s sacrifice; it is not offered to them, because they themselves are also this sacrifice.

The mystery continues:
chunks.notes: Printed sigla: “(VIGILIUS.)” and “(AUG., de Civ. Dei, l. XXII, c. 10.)”. The printed citation “(IV Reg. XXXI, 6)” is rendered as printed. It appears corrupt: Fourth Kings has no chapter thirty-one, and the quotation corresponds to Fourth Kings, chapter nineteen, verse thirty-four in the Vulgate, equivalent to Second Kings, chapter nineteen, verse thirty-four in many modern Bibles.  Printed 'altaria inquibus' is a word-division misprint for 'in quibus'.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 58. «Hanc igitur oblationem servitutis nostrae,» etc., usque «Per Christum Dominum nostrum.» Et in his verbis unitas Ecclesiae offerentis ostenditur, quando in illa sacrosancta oblatione communis servitus exhibetur Deo tam a sacerdotibus quam a cuncta familia domus Dei. (Ibid., l b. X, cap. 19.) Haec autem est servitus quae nulli alii debetur, nec sanctis angelis, nec sanctis animabus, nisi uni Deo vivo et vero, de quo nobis praecipitur: «Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et illi soli servies» (Matth. IV, 10). Etsi enim ab homine sit vel offertur, tamen sacrificium res divina [Col. 0051A] est, unde et alibi divina lege praecipitur: «Sacrificans diis eradicabitur, nisi Domino soli.» Unde merito illi in coelestibus sedibus constituti immortales et beati, quia nos mortales et miseros, ut immortales beatique simus misericorditer diligunt; nolunt nos sibi sacrificare, sed ei cujus et ipsi nobiscum sacrificium se esse noverunt. Cum ipsis enim sumus una civitas Dei (dicitur in psalmo: «Gloriosa dicta sunt de te, civitas Dei»), cujus pars in nobis peregrinatur, pars in illis opitulatur. Oratur itaque Deus ut hanc oblationem, quam illi soli debita servitute defert Ecclesia placatus accipiat. Haec est enim vera oblatio, in qua Filius offertur, Pater reconciliatur; quia, ut Apostolus ait, «Christus dilexit nos, et tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem et hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis.» Et tali oblatione placatus dies nostros, quibus in hac mortalitate inter diversas tentationes et impugnationes vivimus, in sua pace disponat, ita omnia sua pietate moderando, ut ferre possimus, ut ab ejus pace non deficiamus; ut, etsi in mundo pressuram habemus, in illo pacem habeamus. Finito autem hujus mortalitatis cursu, ab aeterna damnatione [Col. 0051B] ereptos, in electorum suorum grege nos annumerare dignetur. (GREG.) Quia ipsa quoque perennis regni praedestinatio ita est ab Omnipotente disposita, ut ad hoc electi ex labore perveniant, quatenus postulando mereantur accipere, quod eis omnipotens Deus ante saecula disposuit donare. Sequitur in mysterio.
chunks.english:
“Therefore this offering of our service,” and so on, as far as, “Through Christ our Lord.”

In these words the unity of the Church as she makes the offering is shown. For in that most holy offering, one common service is rendered to God both by the priests and by the whole family of God’s household. [Augustine]

This is the service owed to no one else: not to the holy angels, not to holy souls, but only to the one living and true God. About him we are commanded, as the Gospel of Matthew, chapter four, verse ten, says: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone.”

For even if a sacrifice is offered by a human being, sacrifice is still a divine reality. That is why the divine law also commands elsewhere: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, unless he sacrifices to the Lord alone.”

And so those immortal and blessed beings who dwell in the heavenly places are right to refuse sacrifices from us. In mercy they love us, who are mortal and miserable, so that we may become immortal and blessed. They do not want us to sacrifice to them, but to him whose sacrifice they know both they and we belong to. For together with them we are one city of God—as it says in the psalm, “Glorious things are said of you, city of God.” One part of this city is still on pilgrimage in us; another part already helps us in them.

So God is asked to be appeased and to accept this offering, which the Church brings to him alone in the service that is owed to him. For this is the true offering: in it the Son is offered, and the Father is reconciled. As the Apostle says, “Christ loved us and handed himself over for us, as an offering and a sacrifice to God, in the fragrance of sweetness.”

And, appeased by such an offering, may God order our days in his peace—the days in which we live in this mortal life amid many temptations and attacks. May he govern everything by his loving care, so that we can bear it, so that we do not fall away from his peace, and so that, even though we have distress in the world, we may have peace in him. And when the course of this mortal life is finished, may he rescue us from eternal damnation and graciously count us among the flock of his chosen ones. [Gregory]

For even the predestination of that everlasting kingdom has been arranged by the Almighty in such a way that the chosen reach it through labor. By asking, they are made worthy to receive what almighty God arranged before all ages to give them.

The mystery continues:

chunks.latin: 59. «Quam oblationem tu, Deus, in omnibus,» etc. Oratur omnipotens Deus ut oblationem suis sacris altaribus impositam et tantis precibus commendatam, ipse per virtutem Spiritus descendentis ita legitimam et perfectam eucharistiam efficiat, ut in omnibus sit ascripta, id est in numerum placitorum sibi numeretur recepta; sit etiam rata, id est immobili firmitate perpetua. Hoc namque dicitur ratum, quod est [Col. 0051C] immobili ratione firmum et inconvulsum. Sit quoque ejusdem Spiritus sancti operante virtute, rationabilis et per haec omnia singulariter Deo grata et acceptabilis, ut, quamvis de simplicibus terrae frugibus sumpta, divinae benedictionis ineffabili potentia efficiatur corpus et sanguis unigeniti Filii Dei, sicut ipse testatur: «Caro mea vere est cibus, et sanguis meus vere est potus» (Joan., VI, 56), ut per hunc cibum et potum impleatur in mentibus sumentium quod ipse promittit dicens: «Sicut me misit vivens Pater, et ego vivo propter Patrem; et qui manducat me, et ipse vivet propter me» (Ibid., LVIII). Haec est ergo vera et aeterna hostia, quia vera et aeterna est virtus, vera et aeterna per eam perficitur salus. Est enim novi et aeterni Testamenti. Haec est rationabilis hostia, plena videlicet [Col. 0051D] rationis, plena mysterii, quae non corporali mactatione, ut in veteribus sacrificiis fiebat, sed spiritali ratione celebratur, et fidei puritate exhibetur, juxta Apostolum fidelem praecipientem rationabile obsequium nostrum. Ut enim hoc Apostolus diceret, utique de spiritali sacrificio loquebatur. Unde et alibi ait: «Necesse est ergo exemplaria quidem coelestium his mundari» (Hebr. IX, 23); ipsa autem coelestia melioribus hostiis quam istis. Ut enim corda fidelium fierent coelestia, et, sicut portaverant imaginem terreni, portarent et imaginem ejus qui de coelis est, et qualis coelestis tales fierent et coelestes, non brutorum animalium cruore, sed rationabili sanguinis Christi cruore mundari debuerunt; qui, ut idem [Col. 0052A] testatur Apostolus, per Spiritum sanctum semetipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo. Hoc namque nobis in sacramento corporis et sanguinis Filii Dei quotidie instauratur. (AUG., lib. XX contra Faust, c. 13.) Hoc corpus et hic sanguis non in spicis et in sarmentis colligitur, sed certa consecratione mysticus fit. Nobis non nascitur, cum panis et vini creatura in sacramentum carnis et sanguinis ejus ineffabili Spiritus sanctificatione transfertur. Quod autem non ita fit, quamvis sit panis et calix, alimentum est refectionis, non sacramentum religionis, quo divinum altare Christus implevit. Invitavit ergo Dominus servos, et praeparavit eis cibum seipsum. Quis audeat manducare Dominum suum? Et tamen ait: «Qui manducat me, vivit propter me» (Joan. VI, 58). Quando [Col. 0052B] Christus manducatur, vita manducatur, non occiditur ut manducetur, sed mortuos vivificat, quando manducatur. Reficit, sed non deficit; manducatur Christus, vivit manducatus, quia resurrexit occisus; nec, quando manducamus, partes de illo facimus; et quidem in sacramento sic fit, per partes manducatur in sacramento, et manet integer totus in coelo, manet integer totus in corde suo. Sequitur in mysterio.
chunks.english:
“Which offering you, O God, in all things,” and so on.

Almighty God is asked to make the offering placed upon his holy altars, and commended by so many prayers, into a lawful and perfect Eucharist by the power of the Spirit who descends. It is to be “ascribed” in all things—that is, received and counted among the things pleasing to him. It is also to be “ratified”—that is, established forever with unshakable firmness. For something is called ratified when it is firm and unmoved by an unchangeable principle.

And by the working power of the same Holy Spirit, this offering is to be “reasonable.” Through all these qualities it becomes uniquely pleasing and acceptable to God. Though taken from the simple fruits of the earth, by the unspeakable power of divine blessing it becomes the body and blood of the only-begotten Son of God. He himself bears witness to this when he says, in the Gospel of John, chapter six, verse fifty-six: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Through this food and drink, what he promises is fulfilled in the minds of those who receive it. He says, in the Gospel of John, chapter six, verse fifty-eight: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so the one who eats me will also live because of me.”

This, then, is the true and eternal sacrifice, because its power is true and eternal, and through it true and eternal salvation is accomplished. For it belongs to the new and eternal covenant. This is the reasonable sacrifice: full of reason, full of mystery. It is not celebrated by bodily slaughter, as happened in the sacrifices of old, but by spiritual meaning; and it is offered in the purity of faith, in keeping with the faithful Apostle’s command that our worship should be reasonable. For when the Apostle said this, he was certainly speaking about spiritual sacrifice.

That is why he says elsewhere, in Paul’s letter to the Hebrews, chapter nine, verse twenty-three: “It is necessary, then, for the copies of the heavenly things to be cleansed with these”; but the heavenly realities themselves must be cleansed with better sacrifices than these. The hearts of the faithful had to become heavenly. Just as they had borne the image of the earthly man, they had to bear also the image of the one who is from heaven; and as he is heavenly, they too had to become heavenly. Therefore they had to be cleansed, not by the blood of irrational animals, but by the reasonable blood of Christ. As the same Apostle testifies, Christ offered himself spotless to God through the Holy Spirit.

This is renewed for us every day in the sacrament of the body and blood of the Son of God. [Augustine]

This body and this blood are not gathered from ears of grain or from vine branches; rather, by a definite consecration they become mystical. They do not grow naturally for us, since the created reality of bread and wine is transferred into the sacrament of his flesh and blood by the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit. But what is not made in this way, even though it is bread and cup, is food for bodily refreshment, not the sacrament of religion with which Christ filled the divine altar.

So the Lord invited his servants, and he prepared food for them: himself. Who would dare to eat his Lord? And yet he says, in the Gospel of John, chapter six, verse fifty-eight: “The one who eats me lives because of me.”

When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. He is not killed so that he may be eaten; rather, when he is eaten, he gives life to the dead. He refreshes, but he is not used up. Christ is eaten, and, having been eaten, he lives, because, having been killed, he rose again. Nor, when we eat, do we divide him into pieces. And yet in the sacrament it happens in this way: in the sacrament he is eaten in portions, and still he remains whole and entire in heaven, and whole and entire in his own heart.

The mystery continues:

chunks.latin: 60. «Qui, pridie quam pateretur, accepit panem,» etc., usque ad «haec quotiescunque feceritis, in mei memoriam facietis.» Unde universalis Ecclesia, ut jugem memoriam Domini et Redemptoris sui celebret, ipse Dominus tradidit apostolis, et apostoli generaliter omni Ecclesiae in his verbis, sine quibus nulla lingua, [Col. 0052C] nulla regio, nulla civitas, id est nulla pars Ecclesiae catholicae conficere potest, id est consecrare sacramentum corporis et sanguinis Domini, quod Apostolus manifeste demonstrat ad Corinthios, ubi dicit: «Ego enim accepi a Domino quod et tradidi vobis, quoniam Dominus Jesus in qua nocte tradebatur accepit panem,» etc. Christi ergo virtute et verbis iste panis et calix ab initio consecratus est; Christi ergo virtute et verbis semper consecratur et consecrabitur. Ille in suis sacerdotibus quotidie loquitur. Illius sermo est qui coelestia sacramenta sanctificat. Illi funguntur officio, ille majestate divinae potestatis operatur. Ipse est enim ille verus Melchisedech, qui haec sancta sacrificia, quae ille tunc in mysterio praefiguravit, per oblationem sui corporis suique sanguinis adimplevit. Ipse ea Spiritus paracliti virtute et coelesti benedictione sanctum corpus et sanguinem suum esse perficit. [Col. 0052D] Quod autem de pane ait: «Accipite et manducate ex hoc omnes;» similiter et de calice: «Accipite et bibite ex eo omnes,» commendatio est unitatis et pacis, ut per hoc mysterium Christo participantes, unum omnes simus in illo, sicut Apostolus affirmat, dicens: «Non est Judaeus neque Graecus; non est servus neque liber, non est masculus neque femina; omnes enim vos unum estis in Christo Jesu» (Gal. III, 28). Hanc namque unitatem in communicatione hujus sacramenti alibi commendat dicens: «Calix benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est; et panis quem frangimus, nonne participatio corporis Christi est» (I Cor. X, 16)? Quoniam unus panis, unum corpus multi sumus omnes, qui de uno pane participamus. [Col. 0053A] Tanta enim est Ecclesiae in Christo unitas, ut quomodo una fides et unum baptisma et unum altare, de quo ait Isaias: «Erit altare Domini in medio terrae Aegypti» (Isa. XIX, 19); ita unus ubique sit panis corporis Christi, et unus calix sanguinis ejus. Unde et Ecclesia ex traditione apostolorum his verbis consecrans mysterium sacri corporis et sanguinis Domini, designanter dicit Dominum dixisse apostolis: «Accipite et manducate ex hoc omnes; hoc est enim corpus meum. Simili modo posteaquam coenatum est, accipiens et hunc praeclarum calicem.» Attendat fidelis quisque, quid est quod dicit «hunc,» videlicet quia calix, quem sacerdos catholicus sacrificat, non est alius, nisi ipse quem Dominus apostolis tradidit. Sicut ergo de sanguine, sic quoque de corpore sentiendum [Col. 0053B] et tenendum est. Quod autem «praeclarum calicem» dicit, manifeste de psalmo sumptum est, ubi canitur: «Et calix tuus inebrians quam praeclarus est» (Psal. XXII, 5)! Et vere praeclarus, quo sanguis offertur immaculatus, nulla peccati nebula tactus. Hoc poculo fidelium inebriatur affectus, ut laetitiam induat de remissione peccati. Hac ebrietate animus non confunditur, sed consecratur.
chunks.english:
“Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread,” and so on, as far as, “As often as you do these things, you will do them in memory of me.”

The Lord himself handed on these words to the apostles, and the apostles handed them on to the whole Church, so that the universal Church might celebrate the continual memorial of her Lord and Redeemer. Without these words, no language, no region, no city—that is, no part of the catholic Church—can perform, that is, consecrate, the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord. The Apostle shows this clearly in his first letter to the Corinthians, where he says: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night he was handed over, took bread,” and so on.

Therefore this bread and cup were consecrated from the beginning by the power and words of Christ. By the power and words of Christ they are always consecrated, and always will be consecrated. He speaks every day in his priests. It is his word that sanctifies the heavenly sacraments. They carry out the office; he works by the majesty of divine power.

For he is the true Melchizedek. The holy sacrifices that Melchizedek once prefigured in mystery, Christ fulfilled by the offering of his own body and his own blood. He himself, by the power of the Spirit, the Paraclete, and by heavenly blessing, makes them to be his holy body and blood.

When he says of the bread, “Take and eat from this, all of you,” and similarly of the cup, “Take and drink from it, all of you,” this is a commendation of unity and peace. Through this mystery, by sharing in Christ, all of us are to be one in him. As the Apostle affirms in Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter three, verse twenty-eight: “There is no Jew and no Greek; there is no slave and no free person; there is no male and no female. For all of you are one in Christ Jesus.”

Elsewhere he commends this same unity in the sharing of this sacrament, saying in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter ten, verse sixteen: “The cup of blessing that we bless—is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? And the bread that we break—is it not a participation in the body of Christ?” Because there is one bread, we, though many, are one body, all of us who share in the one bread.

So great is the unity of the Church in Christ that, just as there is one faith, one baptism, and one altar—about which Isaiah says, in the Book of Isaiah, chapter nineteen, verse nineteen, “There will be an altar of the Lord in the middle of the land of Egypt”—so too, everywhere, there is one bread of Christ’s body and one cup of his blood.

Therefore the Church, consecrating the mystery of the Lord’s holy body and blood by these words received from the tradition of the apostles, deliberately says that the Lord said to the apostles: “Take and eat from this, all of you; for this is my body. In the same way, after supper, taking also this glorious chalice.”

Let every believer pay attention to what is meant by the word “this.” The chalice that a catholic priest offers in sacrifice is no other than the very one the Lord handed on to the apostles. What is to be understood and held about the blood must also be understood and held about the body.

And when the prayer says “glorious chalice,” this is clearly taken from the psalm where it is sung, in the Book of Psalms, psalm twenty-two, verse five: “And your cup that intoxicates—how glorious it is!” And truly glorious is the chalice in which spotless blood is offered, touched by no cloud of sin. By this cup the love of the faithful is made drunk, so that it may put on the joy that comes from the forgiveness of sin. By this intoxication the soul is not confused, but consecrated.
chunks.notes: Editorial column markers are omitted from the English. The citation “Psal. XXII, 5” is rendered as printed, “the Book of Psalms, psalm twenty-two, verse five”; in many modern English numbering systems this corresponds to Psalm twenty-three.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 61. Item, quod in his verbis dicitur: «Novi et aeterni Testamenti,» manifestum est, quia in Evangelio non legitur, nisi tantummodo, «Calix sanguinis mei Novi Testamenti,» sed quod hic additur «aeterni» et in propheticis et in apostolicis litteris continetur. Nam in Isaia legimus, promittente Deo fidelibus: «Et feriam vobiscum pactum,» id est testamentum sempiternum. [Col. 0053C] Et in Ezechiele, ubi promittit Ecclesiae: «Et suscitabo tibi pactum sempiternum» (Ezech. XVI, 80). Et Apostolus dicit: «Una enim oblatione consummavit in sempiternum sanctificatos» (Hebr. X, 14). Et iterum: «Deus autem pacis, qui eduxit de mortuis pastorem, Agnum ovium in sanguine Testamenti aeterni Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum» (Hebr. XIII, 20). (AUG.) Ideo ergo sanguis Christi novum est testamentum, quia nova dilectio, qua usque ad mortem in novissimis saeculorum temporibus nos dilexit. Dilectio ista nos innovet, ut simus homines novi, haeredes Testamenti Novi, sicut et apostolus docet, dicens: «Quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum sanctum semetipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo, emundavit conscientiam nostram ab operibus mortuis, ad serviendum»[Col. 0053D] «Deo viventi? Et ideo Novi Testamenti mediator» (Hebr. IX, 14). Per hunc ergo sanguinem Novi Testamenti qui est effusus in remissionem peccatorum, emundavit, id est innovavit conscientiam fidelium, et fiunt iidem fideles juxta eumdem Apostolum haeredes secundum spem vitae aeternae, et repromissionem accipiunt qui vocantur aeternae haereditatis. Et ideo sanguis ille Novi et aeterni est Testamenti, quia quos a vetustate innovat ad aeternam haereditatem perducit. Hinc Zacharias propheta, velut ad ipsum Dominum loquens, ait: «Tu quoque in sanguine Testamenti tui emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu, in quo nunc erat aqua» (Zach. IX, 10): quia videlicet per hujus sanguinis effusionem et antiqui justi spe futurae redemptionis [Col. 0054A] devincti ab inferni claustris educti sunt, et per eumdem etiam omnes credentes a peccatorum vinculis et de lacu miseriae et de luto faecis eripiuntur.
chunks.english: Next, the words, “of the new and eternal covenant,” are easy to explain. In the Gospel we read only this: “the cup of my blood of the new covenant.” But the added word “eternal” is found both in the prophetic writings and in the apostolic writings. For in Isaiah we read God’s promise to the faithful: “I will make a covenant with you,” that is, an everlasting covenant. And in Ezekiel, where God promises the Church: “I will raise up for you an everlasting covenant,” in the book of Ezekiel, chapter sixteen, verse eighty. And the Apostle says: “By one offering he has perfected forever those who have been sanctified,” in the letter to the Hebrews, chapter ten, verse fourteen. And again: “The God of peace, who brought back from the dead the shepherd, the Lamb of the sheep, in the blood of the eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus Christ,” in the letter to the Hebrews, chapter thirteen, verse twenty. [Augustine] Therefore the blood of Christ is the new covenant because it is the new love by which, in the last ages of the world, he loved us even to death. May that love make us new, so that we may be new people, heirs of the New Covenant, just as the Apostle teaches when he says: “How much more has the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleansed our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God? And therefore he is the mediator of the New Covenant,” in the letter to the Hebrews, chapter nine, verse fourteen. So by this blood of the New Covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of sins, he cleansed—that is, he renewed—the conscience of the faithful. And those same faithful, according to the same Apostle, become heirs in hope of eternal life, and those who are called receive the promised eternal inheritance. And this is why that blood belongs to the new and eternal covenant: it renews people from oldness and leads them into an eternal inheritance.
