Hence the prophet Zechariah, speaking as if to the Lord himself, says: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent out your prisoners from the pit in which there was now water,” in the book of Zechariah, chapter nine, verse ten. For through the pouring out of this blood, even the righteous people of old, held bound in hope of the redemption still to come, were brought out from the prison of the underworld; and through that same blood, all believers are rescued from the bonds of sins, from the pit of misery, and from the mud of filth.
chunks.notes: Printed source siglum: (AUG.). The citation printed as Ezekiel 16:80 is impossible in standard chapter numbering; the wording corresponds to Ezekiel 16:60, but the printed reference has been spoken as given. In Hebrews 13:20 the printed Latin reads “pastorem, Agnum ovium”; the usual biblical text is “pastorem magnum ovium,” “the great shepherd of the sheep.” The translation keeps the printed wording. The Zechariah reference is printed as Zechariah 9:10, though the quoted wording corresponds more closely to Zechariah 9:11; the printed Latin also reads “nunc erat aqua,” “there was now water,” where the biblical text has “non erat aqua,” “there was no water.” The translation follows the printed Latin.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 62. Item, quod hic dicitur «mysterium fidei,» et in illis verbis Domini quibus mysterium corporis et sanguinis sui tradidit, non legitur, videtur de alio loco Evangelii sumptum esse, ubi, secundum Joannem, de hoc eodem sacramento quibusdam discipulis non credentibus loquens ait: «Verba quae ego locutus sum vobis, Spiritus et vita sunt, sed sunt quidam ex vobis qui non credunt» (Joan. VI, 64, 65). Ostendit enim se magnum dixisse mysterium, cum ait: «Verba quae ego locutus sum, Spiritus et vita sunt.» Cum autem adjungit: «Sed sunt quidam ex vobis qui non credunt,» ostendit illud mysterium non esse [Col. 0054B] nisi fidei et fidelium, qui illa verba fideliter audiunt; et ideo eis spiritus et vita sunt: quia eos spiritaliter intellecta vivificant (AUG., lib. I de peccat. Meritis et Remis., c. 24). Aut certe haec verba de Apostolo sumpta sunt, ubi ait: «Habentes mysterium fidei in conscientia pura» (I Tim. III, 9), quia sicut sacramentum sanctae Trinitatis, ita et sacramentum Dominicae passionis et mortis, quod illa oblatione frequentatur aequaliter necessarium ad salutem, aequaliter in conscientia pura est sumendum ac retinendum. Quod etiam in baptismate celebratur, docente eodem Apostolo ac dicente: «Quicunque enim baptizati sumus in Christo Jesu, in morte ipsius baptizati sumus.» Totum ergo quod in hac oblatione Dominici corporis et sanguinis agitur, mysterium est: aliud enim videtur, [Col. 0054C] aliud intelligitur: quod videtur speciem habet corporalem, quod intelligitur fructum habet spiritualem. Sciendum vero quod eumdem calicem Domini sanguinis juxta observantiam Ecclesiae catholicae ab apostolis traditam, nisi mistum aqua offerri non licet, quia vinum fuit redemptionis nostrae mysterium, cum ait: «Non bibam a modo de hoc genimine vitis» (Marc. XIV, 25), et de latere ejus quod lancea transfixum est, aquaque cum sanguine egressa vinum de vera carnis ejus vite cum aqua expressum ostendit. Haec sunt enim sacramenta Ecclesiae, sine quibus ad vitam quae vere vita est non intratur. Ille sanguis in remissionem fusus est peccatorum, aqua illa salutare temperat poculum: haec et lavacrum praestat et potum.
chunks.english: Next, the phrase used here, “the mystery of faith,” is not found in the Lord’s own words when he handed on the mystery of his body and blood. It seems to have been taken from another place in the Gospel, where, according to John, he speaks about this same sacrament to some disciples who did not believe. He says: “The words that I have spoken to you are Spirit and life; but there are some of you who do not believe,” in the Gospel of John, chapter six, verses sixty-four through sixty-five. He shows that he had spoken a great mystery when he says: “The words that I have spoken are Spirit and life.” And when he adds, “But there are some of you who do not believe,” he shows that this mystery belongs only to faith and to the faithful, who hear those words faithfully. For that reason the words are Spirit and life for them: understood spiritually, they give them life. [Augustine] Or else these words come from the Apostle, where he says: “holding the mystery of faith in a pure conscience,” in Paul’s first letter to Timothy, chapter three, verse nine. For just as the sacrament of the Holy Trinity is necessary for salvation, so also the sacrament of the Lord’s passion and death, which is celebrated again and again in that offering, is equally necessary for salvation, and must equally be received and held in a pure conscience. This is also celebrated in baptism, as the same Apostle teaches when he says: “All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.” Therefore everything that happens in this offering of the Lord’s body and blood is a mystery. One thing is seen; another thing is understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit. We must also know that, according to the practice of the Catholic Church handed down from the apostles, that same cup of the Lord’s blood may not be offered unless it is mixed with water. For wine was the mystery of our redemption when he said: “I will no longer drink of this fruit of the vine,” in the Gospel of Mark, chapter fourteen, verse twenty-five. And from his side, pierced by the lance, water came out together with blood; this showed wine pressed out, together with water, from the true vine of his flesh. These are the sacraments of the Church, without which no one enters into the life that is truly life. That blood was poured out for the forgiveness of sins. That water tempers the saving cup. It provides both washing and drink.
chunks.notes: Printed source siglum: (AUG., lib. I de peccat. Meritis et Remis., c. 24). The citation printed as John 6:64–65 is spoken as given, though the quoted sentence begins with wording normally associated with John 6:63. The baptism quotation is from Romans 6:3, but no biblical citation is printed in the source at that point.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 63. Hoc totum Dominicae oblationis mysterium [Col. 0054D] quanta pietate et amore agendum est et accipiendum sit, commendat nobis ipse Dominus dicendo: «Haec quotiescunque feceritis, in mei memoriam facietis» (Luc. XXII, 19). Quod exponens Apostolus ait: «Quoties enim manducabitis panem hunc, et calicem bibetis, mortem Domini annuntiabitis, donec veniat» (I Cor. XI, 26). Illius ergo panis et calicis oblatio mortis Christi est commemoratio, et annuntiatio, quae non tam verbis quam mysteriis ipsis agitur, per quae nostris mentibus mors illa pretiosa, altius et fortius commendatur. Quid est enim mortis Christi commemoratio, nisi charitatis ejus commendatio, quam nobis beatus evangelista Joannes commendans, ait: «Sciens Jesus quia venit hora ejus, ut transeat a hoc»[Col. 0055A] «mundo ad Patrem, cum dilexisset suos qui erant in mundo, in finem dilexit» (Joan. XIII, 1), id est usque ad mortem eum illa dilectio perduxit, quia tantum dilexit eos ut moreretur propter eos. Hoc enim testatus est, dicens: «Majorem hac dilectionem nemo habet, quam ut animam suam quis ponat pro amicis suis» (Joan. XV, 13). Propterea et iturus ad passionem, et per resurrectionis et ascensionis gloriam discessurus e mundo, hoc sacramentum ultimum discipulis tradidit, ut memoriam tantae charitatis, per quam solam salvamur, arctius eorum mentibus infigeret; quatenus semper memores simus, et quales et quantum ab eo dilecti simus; quales, ne de nobis gloriemur; quantum, ut de illo speremus; quod utrumque diligenter Apostolus imponit et inculcat, [Col. 0055B] dicens: «Ut quid enim Christus, cum adhuc infirmi essemus, secundum tempus pro impiis mortuus est» (Rom. V, 6)? Et post paululum: «Commendat autem,» inquit, «suam charitatem Deus in nobis, quoniam si, cum adhuc peccatores essemus, Christus pro nobis mortuus est, multo magis justificati nunc in sanguine ipsius salvi erimus ab ira per ipsum. Si enim cum inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus, multo magis reconciliati salvi erimus in vita ipsius» (Rom. VIII, 9, 10). Hoc ergo agendum, hoc frequentandum commendavit, quo usque ipse veniat in fine saeculi, quando erit sanctorum requies, non adhuc in sacramento spei, quo in hoc tempore consociatur Ecclesia, quandiu bibitur quod de latere Christi emanavit, sed jam ipsa perfectione salutis aeternae, [Col. 0055C] cum tradetur regnum Deo et Patri, ut in illa perspicua contemplatione incommutabilis veritatis, nullis mysteriis corporalibus egeamus. (GREG.) Haec namque singulariter victima ab aeterno interitu animam salvat, quae illam nobis mortem Unigeniti per mysterium reparat. Qui, licet surgens a mortuis, jam non moritur, et mors ei ultra non dominabitur; tamen, in se ipso immortaliter atque incorruptibiliter vivens, pro nobis iterum in hoc mysterio sacrae oblationis immolatur. Ejus quippe ibi corpus sumitur, ejus caro in populi salute partitur. Ejus sanguis non jam in manus infidelium funditur. Hinc ergo pensemus quale sit pro nobis hoc sacrificium, quod pro absolutione nostra passionem unigeniti Filii semper imitatur. Sequitur in mysterio:
chunks.english: The Lord himself teaches us with what devotion and love this whole mystery of the Lord’s offering must be performed and received, when he says: “As often as you do these things, you will do them in memory of me,” in the Gospel of Luke, chapter twenty-two, verse nineteen. Explaining this, the Apostle says: “As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you will proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes,” in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, verse twenty-six. So the offering of that bread and cup is the remembrance and proclamation of Christ’s death. This is carried out not so much by words as by the mysteries themselves; through them that precious death is commended to our minds more deeply and more powerfully. For what is the remembrance of Christ’s death, if not the commendation of his love? The blessed evangelist John commends that love to us when he says: “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end,” in the Gospel of John, chapter thirteen, verse one. That means: this love led him all the way to death, because he loved them so much that he died for them. He himself bore witness to this when he said: “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends,” in the Gospel of John, chapter fifteen, verse thirteen. Therefore, as he was about to go to his passion, and as he was about to depart from the world through the glory of his resurrection and ascension, he handed on this sacrament last of all to his disciples. He did this so that he might fix more firmly in their minds the memory of so great a love—the love by which alone we are saved. In this way we may always remember both what kind of people we were when he loved us, and how greatly he loved us: what kind of people, so that we may not boast about ourselves; how greatly, so that we may place our hope in him. The Apostle carefully teaches and presses both points when he says: “For why did Christ, when we were still weak, die at the appointed time for the ungodly?” in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter five, verse six. And a little later he says: “But God commends his love in us, because, if Christ died for us while we were still sinners, much more, now that we have been justified in his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him. For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, now reconciled, shall we be saved in his life,” in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eight, verses nine through ten. This, then, is what he commanded to be done and repeated until he himself comes at the end of the age. Then the saints will have rest—not still in the sacrament of hope, by which the Church is joined together in this present time, as long as she drinks what flowed from the side of Christ, but already in the full perfection of eternal salvation. Then the kingdom will be handed over to God the Father, and in that clear contemplation of unchangeable truth we will need no bodily mysteries. [Gregory] For this victim, in a unique way, saves the soul from eternal destruction, because through the mystery it renews for us the death of the Only-Begotten Son. Although he has risen from the dead and now dies no more, and death will no longer have dominion over him, nevertheless he lives in himself immortally and incorruptibly, and yet for us he is again sacrificed in this mystery of the sacred offering. For there his body is received; there his flesh is divided for the salvation of the people. His blood is no longer poured into the hands of unbelievers. From this, then, let us consider what this sacrifice is for us: for our absolution, it always imitates the passion of the only-begotten Son. The mystery continues:
chunks.notes: Printed source siglum: (GREG.). The reference printed as Romans 8:9–10 is spoken as given, though the quoted material corresponds to Romans 5:8–10.  Printed 'ut transeat a hoc mundo' is an evident misprint for 'ab hoc' (Vulgate 'ex hoc'); translated 'to pass from this world'.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 0055D] 64. «Unde et memores nos servi tui,» etc., usque ad «calicem salutis perpetuae.» Quia Dominus et Salvator noster mysterium suae mortis, quam pro nostra omniumque salute suscepit, tanta pietate memoriae fidelium commendavit, ut per oblationem et participationem sui corporis et sanguinis eamdem vivificam mortem suam nos annuntiare voluerit, donec ipse veniat in majestate de coelis, quid dignius aut salubrius fieri potest, quam ut haec veneranda mysteria frequentando memores sint pariter sacerdotes et populus, universa videlicet Ecclesia, beatae passionis ejus. Et vere beatae, quae sine peccato suscepta, totius mundi peccata delevit, et quia non solum, ut Apostolus ait: [Col. 0056A] «Mortuus est propter delicta nostra,» sed etiam «resurrexit propter justificationem nostram» (Rom. IV, 25), ac sic mortem nostram moriendo destruxit, et vitam resurgendo reparavit, memores simus resurrectionis quoque ejus ab inferis,
chunks.english:
“Therefore, remembering, we your servants,” and so on, as far as, “the chalice of everlasting salvation.”

Our Lord and Savior entrusted to the memory of the faithful the mystery of his death, which he accepted for our salvation and for the salvation of all. He did this with such loving care that, through the offering and sharing of his body and blood, he wanted us to proclaim that same life-giving death until he himself comes in majesty from heaven.

So what could be more worthy, or more healing, than this: that by celebrating these venerable mysteries often, the priests and the people together—that is, the whole Church—remember his blessed passion? And it truly is blessed. Though he took it on without sin, it wiped away the sins of the whole world. For, as the Apostle says, not only “he died for our trespasses,” but also “he rose for our justification,” in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter four, verse twenty-five.

And so, by dying, he destroyed our death; by rising, he restored our life. Therefore we should also remember his resurrection from the dead.
chunks.notes: The column markers are editorial and are not spoken in the English. The liturgical lemma is abbreviated in the source, so the translation keeps “and so on” and “as far as,” without completing the prayer.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: per quam, spoliato inferno, sicut per prophetam praedixerat: «Ero mors tua, o mors; morsus tuus ero, inferne,» implevit in se quod antea fuerat prophetatum: «Quoniam non derelinques animam meam in inferno, nec dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem;» et, quoniam resurgens a mortuis factus est primitiae dormientium et primogenitus mortuorum, quia jam non moritur, et mors ei ultra non dominabitur, et assumptus in coelum, sedet a dextris Dei, simus memores etiam gloriosae ascensionis ejus, quando, gratulantibus angelis et omni militia coelestis exercitus in ejus laudibus concrepante, implevit quod in psalmo canitur: «Ascendit Deus in jubilatione, et Dominus in voce tubae.» Unde et in alio psalmo coelestium virtutum voces introducuntur in ejus gloriosa ascensione admirando interrogantium et congratulando respondentium, cum interrogantes dicunt: «Quis est iste rex gloriae?» et respondentes adjungunt: «Dominus fortis et potens, Dominus potens in praelio.» Et iterum interrogant: «Quis est iste rex gloriae?» et respondent: «Dominus virtutum ipse est rex gloriae.»
chunks.english:
Through that resurrection, once hell had been despoiled, he fulfilled in himself what he had foretold through the prophet: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell.” He also fulfilled what had earlier been prophesied: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor let your holy one see corruption.”

And because, rising from the dead, he became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep and the firstborn from the dead; because he no longer dies, and death will no longer have dominion over him; and because he was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God—we should also remember his glorious ascension.

At that ascension, while the angels rejoiced and the whole army of heaven rang out his praises, he fulfilled what is sung in the psalm: “God has gone up with a shout of joy, and the Lord with the sound of a trumpet.” So too, in another psalm, the voices of the heavenly powers are brought in at his glorious ascension: they ask in wonder, and they answer in celebration. The questioners say, “Who is this King of glory?” And the answerers add, “The Lord, strong and mighty; the Lord, mighty in battle.” Again they ask, “Who is this King of glory?” And they answer, “The Lord of powers: he is the King of glory.”
chunks.notes: Several biblical quotations in this passage are given without printed references in the source; none have been added in the English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Haec est enim tota salus nostra et vita, si incessanter ejus memores simus, et illi soli nos deberi cognoscamus, cujus passione firmati, cujus vulnere sanati, cujus sanguine mundati, morte vivificati, resurrectione coexcitati, ascensione in coelis glorificati sumus; quia et ideo pretium redemptionis nostrae in sacramento Dominici corporis et sanguinis celebramus, ut semper illud fideliter meditemur, quod Apostolus monet dicens: «Et non estis vestri; empti enim estis pretio magno.» Memores igitur Dominicae passionis, resurrectionis et ascensionis, tam sacerdotes quam plebs fidelis offerunt praeclarae, id est praecellenti et gloriosae majestati Dei, non de suo, sed de ejus donis ac datis, juxta quod scriptum est: Et quae de manu tua accepimus, dedimus tibi. Ipse est enim qui educit panem de terra, et praestat ut vinum laetificet cor hominis. Ex his ergo creaturae Dei fructibus, id est bonitatis et pietatis ejus muneribus, offert illi Ecclesia in mysterio Dominici corporis et sanguinis vere hostiam puram, hostiam sanctam, hostiam immaculatam. Quae trina repetitio tanti [Col. 0056B] mysterii est laudatio, et laudando commendatio, et commendando piae devotionis excitatio. Haec namque hostia corpus et sanguis ejus, ut beatus Petrus ait, «agni incontaminati et immaculati Christi.»
chunks.english:
For this is our whole salvation and our whole life: to remember him without ceasing, and to know that we belong to him alone. By his passion we have been strengthened; by his wound, healed; by his blood, cleansed; by his death, brought to life; by his resurrection, raised up with him; and by his ascension, glorified in heaven.

That is why we celebrate the price of our redemption in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood: so that we may always meditate faithfully on the Apostle’s warning, “You are not your own; for you were bought at a great price.”

Therefore, remembering the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension, both the priests and the faithful people offer to the excellent majesty of God—that is, to his surpassing and glorious majesty—not anything of their own, but gifts that come from his own gifts and grants. As Scripture says: “What we have received from your hand, we have given back to you.” For he is the one who brings forth bread from the earth, and grants that wine should gladden the human heart.

So from these fruits of God’s creation—that is, from the gifts of his goodness and loving care—the Church offers him, in the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, what is truly a pure victim, a holy victim, an unblemished victim. This threefold repetition praises so great a mystery; by praising it, it commends it to us; and by commending it, it stirs up loving devotion. For this victim is his body and blood, which, as blessed Peter says, belong to “Christ, the spotless and unblemished lamb.”
chunks.notes: The quotation “You are not your own; for you were bought at a great price” appears without a printed biblical reference in the source. The column marker is editorial and is not spoken.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Quam vero hostiam puram, sanctam et immaculatam offert Ecclesia, nisi quam a Domino accepit? id est panem sanctum vitae aeternae, et calicem salutis perpetuae. In hoc enim pane sumentibus vita aeterna est, sicut ipse Dominus panis vivus et panis vitae de se ipso ait: «Ego sum panis vivus qui de coelo descendi» (Joan. VI, 51). Et iterum: «Panis enim Dei est qui descendit de coelo et dat vitam mundo» (Ibid., 33). Et alio loco dicit: «Qui manducat hunc panem, vivet in aeternum» (Ibid., 59). Et quod iste sit panis corporis [Col. 0056C] sui, ipse exponit dicendo: «Et panis quem ego dabo, caro mea est pro mundi vita» (Ibid., 52). Ergo et calix sanguinis ejus, calix est salutis aeternae, quia sanguis ille pro multis effusus est in remissionem peccatorum, ut salvum faceret populum suum a peccatis eorum. De hoc canitur in psalmo: «Calicem salutaris accipiam et nomen Domini invocabo» (Psal. CXV, 13).
chunks.english:
But what pure, holy, and unblemished victim does the Church offer, except the one she has received from the Lord? That is, the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation.

For in this bread there is eternal life for those who receive it, as the Lord himself—the living bread and the bread of life—says about himself: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven,” in the Gospel of John, chapter six, verse fifty-one. And again: “For the bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world,” in the same Gospel, chapter six, verse thirty-three. And elsewhere he says: “Whoever eats this bread will live forever,” in the same Gospel, chapter six, verse fifty-nine.

And he explains that this bread is the bread of his body when he says: “And the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world,” in the same Gospel, chapter six, verse fifty-two.

Therefore the chalice of his blood is also the chalice of eternal salvation, because that blood was poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins, so that he might save his people from their sins. About this it is sung in the psalm: “I will take up the chalice of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord,” in the Book of Psalms, Psalm one hundred fifteen, verse thirteen.
chunks.notes: The source prints “Ibid., 59” for “Whoever eats this bread will live forever”; in many modern editions this wording corresponds to the Gospel of John, chapter six, verse fifty-eight. The English speaks the printed reference, as required. The column marker is editorial and is not spoken.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Est enim calix iste salutaris accipienti, et in sacramenti perceptione, et in passionis imitatione, sicut a sanctis martyribus acceptus est. Hunc panem significavit manna, hunc panem tribuit altare Dei. Noverunt fideles corpus Christi, si in Christi corpore homo fuerit, accipiet de Christi spiritu. Sicut autem corpus nostrum sine spiritu non potest vivere, sic non habebit spiritum vitae, nisi qui in Christi [Col. 0056D] corpore fuerit inventus. Qui vult vivere, accedat, credat, vivat Deo de Deo; incorporetur, ut vivificetur. Hoc est enim manducare illam escam, et illum bibere potum, in Christo manere, et illum manentem in se habere, sicut ipse dicit: «Qui manducat meam carnem, et bibit meum sanguinem in me manet, et ego in illo» (Joan. VI, 57). Sequitur in mysterio.
chunks.english:
This chalice brings salvation to the one who receives it: both in receiving the sacrament, and in imitating the passion, as the holy martyrs received it.

Manna signified this bread; the altar of God provides this bread. The faithful know the body of Christ: if a person is in the body of Christ, he will receive from the Spirit of Christ. Just as our own body cannot live without the spirit, so no one will have the Spirit of life unless he is found in Christ’s body.

Whoever wants to live should come near, believe, and live for God from God. Let him be incorporated into Christ, so that he may be made alive. For this is what it means to eat that food and drink that drink: to remain in Christ, and to have Christ remaining in oneself. As the Lord himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him,” in the Gospel of John, chapter six, verse fifty-seven.

The mystery continues:
chunks.notes: The source prints the reference as the Gospel of John, chapter six, verse fifty-seven; in many modern editions this wording corresponds to chapter six, verse fifty-six. The English speaks the printed reference, as required. The column marker is editorial and is not spoken.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 65. «Supra quae propitio ac sereno vultu,» etc., usque «immaculatam hostiam.» Oratur Deus ut super haec munera vitae et salutis, quae praeclarae majestati ejus offeruntur, propitio, id est placabili et sereno vultu respicere dignetur, non quia vultus ejus aliquando obnubilatur et aliquando serenatur, cum ipse sit Pater luminum, ut beatus Jacobus dicit: «Apud quem non est transmutatio, nec vicissitudinis»[Col. 0057A] «obumbratio» (Jac. I, 17). Et beatus Joannes testatur: «Quoniam Deus lux est, et tenebrae in eo non sunt ullae» (I Joan. I, 5). Sed qui semper in lumine est, tunc super nos serenat, ac illuminat vultum suum quando declarat super nos misericordiam, sicut in psalmo orantes dicimus: «Illuminet vultum suum super nos, et misereatur nostri» (Psal. LXVI, 2). Sicut e contrario de quibusdam, qui ejus misericordia indigni sunt, ipse dicit: «Abscondam faciem meam ab eis» (Deut. XXXI, 17). Et iterum quibus se placabilem praebet, promittit dicens: «Et non avertam faciem meam a vobis» (Jerem. III, 12). Unde et beatus Daniel istis ipsis verbis exorat, dicens: «Exaudi, Domine, preces servi tui, illumina faciem tuam super sanctuarium tuum, et propitius intende populum istum, super»[Col. 0057B] «quem invocatum est nomen tuum» (Dan. IX, 17). Neque enim Deus humana forma faciem aut vultum habere putandus est: quia, ut Dominus in Evangelio ait: «Spiritus est Deus, et eos qui adorant eum, in spiritu et veritate oportet adorare» (Joan. IV, 24). Sed facies et vultus Dei praesentia ejus est. Quid est enim facies Dei super nos illuminata, nisi praesentia declarata, cum misericordiam et bonitatem ipsius praesentem nobis adesse sentimus? Sic et respicere Dei visitatio pietatis ejus est, sicut in psalmo orantes dicimus: «Deus virtutum, converte nos, respice de coelo, et vide, et visita vineam istam» (Psal. LXXIX, 15).
chunks.english:
“Look upon these with a gracious and serene countenance,” and so on, as far as “immaculate victim.” Here God is asked to look, with a gracious—that is, a favorable—and serene countenance, upon these gifts of life and salvation, which are being offered to his glorious majesty. This does not mean that his countenance is sometimes clouded over and sometimes made bright. He is, as blessed James says, “the Father of lights, with whom there is no change, nor shadow of variation,” in the letter of James, chapter one, verse seventeen. And blessed John testifies: “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all,” in the first letter of John, chapter one, verse five.

Rather, the One who is always in light makes his face serene over us, and makes it shine upon us, when he shows us his mercy. So we pray in the Psalm: “May he make his face shine upon us, and have mercy on us,” Psalm sixty-six, verse two. By contrast, concerning certain people who are unworthy of his mercy, he himself says: “I will hide my face from them,” Deuteronomy, chapter thirty-one, verse seventeen. And again, to those toward whom he shows himself gracious, he promises: “I will not turn my face away from you,” the book of Jeremiah, chapter three, verse twelve. For this reason blessed Daniel prays in these very words: “Hear, Lord, the prayers of your servant; make your face shine upon your sanctuary, and look favorably upon this people, over whom your name has been invoked,” the book of Daniel, chapter nine, verse seventeen.

Of course, we must not think that God has a face or countenance in a human bodily form. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth,” the Gospel of John, chapter four, verse twenty-four. Instead, God’s face and countenance mean his presence. What is God’s face shining upon us, if not his presence made known, when we sense that his mercy and goodness are present with us? In the same way, for God to “look upon” us means the visitation of his loving-kindness, as we pray in the Psalm: “God of hosts, turn us back; look down from heaven, and see, and visit this vine,” Psalm seventy-nine, verse fifteen.
chunks.notes: Editorial column markers have been omitted from the English. The liturgical lemma is translated according to the work-specific standardization; the abbreviated “etc.” and “usque” are retained as “and so on, as far as.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Oratur itaque omnipotens Deus, ut, placabilis ac propitius factus, sereno vultu, id est declarata bonitatis et pietatis suae praesentia, respiciat dignanter [Col. 0057C] Ecclesiae suae munera, et accepta et beneplacita habeat, sicut munera pueri sui justi Abel, cujus fides et justitia et oblationis acceptio et in lege veteri commendatur, ubi scriptum est: «Et respexit Deus ad Abel et ad munera ejus» (Gen. IV, 4); et in Evangelio dicente Domino: «A sanguine Abel justi usque ad sanguinem Zachariae filii Barachiae» (Matth. XXII, 35); et ab Apostolo, ubi ad Hebraeos scribit: «Fide plurimam hostiam Abel quam Cain obtulit Deo, per quam testimonium consecutus est esse justus, testimonium perhibente muneribus ejus Deo, et per illam defunctus adhuc loquitur» (Hebr. XI, 4), qui non aetate, sed simplicitate et puritate, puer Dei appellatur. Sicut etiam de David, qui mortuus est senex et plenus dierum, tamen in Evangelio dicitur: «Et erexit cornu salutis nobis in domo David pueri sui» (Luc. I, 69). Et, «sicut sacrificium,» inquit, «patriarchae nostri Abrahae.» Utique quod sacrificium in oblationem unigeniti filii Isaac offerens cum Deo holocaustum, quod ita acceptum fuit [Col. 0057D] ut statim mereretur audire: «Per memetipsum juravi, dicit Dominus, quia fecisti rem hanc, et non pepercisti unigenito filio tuo propter me, benedicam tibi» (Gen. XXII, 12), etc. Qui est patriarcha non tantum Israeliticae plebis secundum carnem, sed etiam noster secundum fidem, sicut ei promissum est: «Quia patrem multarum gentium posui te.» Adjungitur adhuc: «Et quod tibi obtulit summus sacerdos tuus Melchisedech,» de quo manifeste scriptum dicit: «Et Melchisedech rex Salem protulit panes et vinum. Erat enim sacerdos Dei altissimi, et benedixit Abraham» (Gen. XIV, 18), cujus sacerdotium et sacrificium tantum magnificatur, ut dicat de eo Apostolus: «Primum quidem Melchisedech, qui interpretatur rex justitiae, deinde rex Salem, quod est rex pacis, sine patre, sine matre, sine genealogia,»[Col. 0058A] «neque initium dierum neque finem habens, assimilatus per omnia Filio Dei, qui manet sacerdos in aeternum» (Hebr. VI, 3).
chunks.english:
So almighty God is being asked to become favorable and gracious, and with a serene countenance—that is, with the revealed presence of his goodness and mercy—to look kindly upon the gifts of his Church, and to receive them as accepted and pleasing, just as he received the gifts of his righteous servant Abel. Abel’s faith, righteousness, and accepted offering are praised both in the Old Law, where it is written, “And God looked upon Abel and his gifts,” Genesis, chapter four, verse four; and in the Gospel, where the Lord says, “From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah,” the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-two, verse thirty-five; and also by the Apostle, when he writes to the Hebrews: “By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain; through it he received testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks,” the letter to the Hebrews, chapter eleven, verse four. Abel is called God’s “puer”—his child or servant—not because of his age, but because of his simplicity and purity. In the same way David, who died old and full of days, is nevertheless spoken of in the Gospel: “He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant,” the Gospel of Luke, chapter one, verse sixty-nine.

And the prayer says, “as the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham.” Surely this refers to the sacrifice he offered when he presented his only-begotten son Isaac as a holocaust to God. That offering was accepted so fully that Abraham at once deserved to hear: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake, I will bless you,” Genesis, chapter twenty-two, verse twelve, and so on. Abraham is patriarch not only of the Israelite people according to the flesh, but also of us according to faith, just as it was promised to him: “For I have made you the father of many nations.”

The prayer then adds: “and the offering which your high priest Melchizedek offered to you.” Scripture says plainly about him: “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth bread and wine; for he was priest of God Most High, and he blessed Abraham,” Genesis, chapter fourteen, verse eighteen. His priesthood and sacrifice are magnified so greatly that the Apostle says of him: “First, Melchizedek, which is interpreted king of righteousness; then also king of Salem, which means king of peace; without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end, made like in every way to the Son of God, who remains a priest forever,” the letter to the Hebrews, chapter six, verse three.
chunks.notes: Editorial column markers have been omitted from the English. The citation printed as the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-two, verse thirty-five appears to correspond to the wording found at the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-three, verse thirty-five; it has nevertheless been spoken as printed. The citation printed as Genesis, chapter twenty-two, verse twelve combines wording associated with Genesis chapter twenty-two, verses twelve and sixteen through seventeen; it has nevertheless been spoken as printed. The citation printed as the letter to the Hebrews, chapter six, verse three appears to correspond to Hebrews chapter seven, verses two through three; it has nevertheless been spoken as printed. “Puer” is rendered contextually as “child or servant” because Florus comments on both age and purity while the liturgical phrase commonly means “servant.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Quod vero post haec omnia subjungitur «sanctum sacrificium, immaculatam hostiam,» ad superiora referendum esse videtur, ubi dictum est: «Super quae propitio ac sereno vultu respicere digneris,» ut ad complendam petitionem subjunctum sit. Hoc autem totum exoratur omnipotens Deus, ut sacrificium Ecclesiae ita acceptum habeat, ut sacrificium justi Abel, et patriarchae Abrahae, et summi sacerdotis Melchisedech; quia et in illis antiquis sacrificiis imago erat hujus veri sacrificii, et hoc ipsum uni Deo auctori utriusque Testamenti et utriusque sacrificii ordinatissima temporum dispositione tunc placebat in praefiguratione venturae veritatis, quod [Col. 0058B] et nunc placet in adimpletione ejusdem veritatis. Nam et in sacrificio Abel, quod de primogenitis ovium et adipibus earum oblatum, sacrificio Cain quod ex terrae fructibus offerebatur, praelatum est, Novi Testamenti fides praefigurabatur, qua innocentia gratiae Deum laudans, Veteris Testamenti terreni operibus anteponitur, et in immolatione unici et dilecti filii Abrahae immolatio ejus praefigurabatur, de quo dicit Pater: «Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacui» (Matth. XVII, 5). Unde ait Apostolus: «Qui proprio Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum» (Rom. VIII, 32). Et sacrificium Melchisedech tam vera erat significatio sacrificii Christi, ut inde praedictum sit: «Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech» [Col. 0058C] (Psal. CIX, 4). Sequitur in mysterio:
chunks.english:
What is added after all this—“a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim”—seems to refer back to the earlier words, “Look upon these with a gracious and serene countenance,” and to have been added to complete the petition. In this whole prayer, then, almighty God is asked to accept the sacrifice of the Church as he accepted the sacrifice of righteous Abel, the sacrifice of the patriarch Abraham, and the sacrifice of the high priest Melchizedek.

For in those ancient sacrifices there was already an image of this true sacrifice. At that time, by the perfectly ordered arrangement of the ages, the one God—the author of both Testaments and of both kinds of sacrifice—was pleased by what prefigured the truth that was to come; and now he is pleased by the fulfillment of that same truth.

In Abel’s sacrifice, offered from the firstborn of the sheep and from their fat, and preferred over Cain’s sacrifice, which was offered from the fruits of the earth, the faith of the New Testament was prefigured: that faith which, praising God in the innocence of grace, is placed before the earthly works of the Old Testament. And in the sacrifice of Abraham’s only and beloved son, there was prefigured the sacrifice of the one about whom the Father says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,” the Gospel of Matthew, chapter seventeen, verse five. Therefore the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all,” Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eight, verse thirty-two. And the sacrifice of Melchizedek was so true a sign of Christ’s sacrifice that it was foretold about Christ: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” Psalm one hundred nine, verse four.

The mystery continues:
chunks.notes: Editorial column markers have been omitted from the English. “Sanctum sacrificium, immaculatam hostiam” is translated literally as “a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim,” matching the quoted liturgical language.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 66. «Supplices te rogamus, omnipotens Deus,» etc. Haec verba mysterii tam profunda, tam mira et stupenda quis comprehendere sufficiat? quis inde digne aliquid loquatur? magis veneranda sunt et pavenda quam discutienda. Beatus tamen Gregorius, idoneus tanti mysterii interpres, in quodam loco aliquid de iis tanquam de re ineffabili pene ineffabiliter loquitur (GREG., l. IV Dialog., 60). Quis enim fidelium, inquit, habere dubium possit, in ipsa immolationis hora ad sacerdotis vocem coelos aperiri, in illo Jesu Christi mysterio angelorum choris adesse, summis ima sociari, terram coelestibus jungi, unum quid ex visibilibus atque invisibilibus fieri?
chunks.english: “Humbly we beseech you, almighty God,” and so on. Who could ever fully grasp words of a mystery so deep, so wonderful, so astonishing? Who could say anything worthy about them? They are more to be reverenced and feared than analyzed. Still, blessed Gregory, a fitting interpreter of so great a mystery, speaks about them in one place almost unspeakably, as one speaks of something beyond words. [Gregory] He says: “What believer could doubt that, at the very hour of the sacrifice, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened; that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the lowest things are joined to the highest; that earth is united with heaven; and that visible and invisible realities become one?”
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “(GREG., l. IV Dialog., 60).” The liturgical lemma is abbreviated with “etc.” and is therefore rendered “and so on,” without completing the prayer.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Idem etiam doctor quomodo accipiendum sit sublime altare Dei in conspectu divinae majestatis ejus quodam loco subtiliter ostendit, exponens illum versiculum psalmi: «Constituite diem solemnem in confrequentationibus usque ad cornu altaris» (Psal. CXVII, 27). Dies, inquit, solemnis est Domino conjunctio cordis nostri; sed tunc in confrequentatione dies solemnis constituitur, cum in lacrymas pio amore ejus assidue mens movetur, cui velut si diceremus: Quandiu ista acturi sumus? quandiu tribulatione afficimur? Illico terminum quousque fieri debeat subjunxit, dicens: «usque ad cornu altaris;» cornu quippe altaris est exaltatio sacrificii interioris, ubi cum venerimus, jam nulla necessitas est ut solemnem diem Domino de nostra lamentatione faciamus. Beatus quoque Augustinus de eodem sublimi altare dicit, exponens versiculum psalmi: «Lavabo inter innocentes manus meas, et circumdabo altare tuum, Domine» (Psal. XXV, 6), sic breviter designat: Munda, inquit, faciam inter innocentes opera mea, quibus amplexabor sublimia tua. Item alio loco (In psal. XLII, n. 5), exponens illum versiculum: «Et introibo ad altare Dei, ad Deum qui laetificat juventutem meam,» de eadem re sic dicit: Est enim quoddam altare invisibile, ad quod non accedit injustus, ille solus accedit qui ad istud securus accedit. Illic inveniet vitam suam, qui in isto discernit causam suam; quale ibi sacrificium est, ipse qui intrat assumetur in holocaustum. Et repetit aliis verbis quid hoc altare sit, ad Dominum inquiens: «Ad Deum qui laetificat juventutem meam.»
chunks.english: The same teacher also explains, with care, how we should understand “the altar of God on high in the sight of his divine majesty.” He is commenting on the verse of the Psalm: “Establish a solemn day in crowded gatherings, as far as the horn of the altar,” Psalm one hundred seventeen, verse twenty-seven. He says: “A solemn day for the Lord is the joining of our heart to him. But that solemn day is established ‘in crowded gatherings’ when the mind, moved continually by devout love for him, is stirred to tears. And as if we were asking, ‘How long will we keep doing this? How long will we be afflicted by suffering?’ the psalm immediately adds the limit to which this must continue, saying: ‘as far as the horn of the altar.’ For the horn of the altar is the exaltation of the inner sacrifice. Once we have reached it, there will no longer be any need for us to make a solemn day for the Lord out of our lamentation.” Blessed Augustine also speaks about this same altar on high. Commenting on the verse of the Psalm, “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around your altar, Lord,” Psalm twenty-five, verse six, he briefly explains it this way: “I will make my works clean among the innocent, and by those works I will embrace your heights.” Again, elsewhere, explaining the verse, “And I will go in to the altar of God, to God who gives joy to my youth,” he says about the same reality: “There is an invisible altar to which no unjust person comes. Only the one who comes safely to this visible altar can come to that one. There he will find his life, if here he examines his cause. As for the kind of sacrifice offered there: the one who enters will himself be taken up as a whole burnt offering.” And Augustine repeats, in other words, what this altar is, saying to the Lord: “To God who gives joy to my youth.”
chunks.notes: The parenthetical reference “(In psal. XLII, n. 5)” is an editorial patristic source reference and is not spoken as a Bible citation. The quotation “Et introibo ad altare Dei…” comes from Psalm forty-two in the Vulgate, but no scriptural reference is printed at that point, so none is added in the English.  'Dies … solemnis est Domino conjunctio cordis nostri' is translated as printed ('the joining of our heart'); the following clause on tears and lamentation suggests that 'conjunctio' may be a misprint for 'compunctio' ('compunction of our heart'), Gregory's usual term, but this is uncertain and the English is unchanged.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Item alibi idem doctor exponens eumdem versiculum, quem et beatus Gregorius: Sic enim est, inquit, in domo illa sempiterna sacrificium laudis, et sacerdos sempiternus est, et altare sempiternum, pacata mens ipsa justorum. Non ergo sufficiat in terra dies ille solemnis quo Agnus occisus est, sed constituite illum in condensis sempiternum, alta et secreta rimantes, quo usque perveniaris, exaltatis a Deo mentibus vestris, usque ad ejus divinitatem. Et quid ibi aliud, nisi laudes cantabimus? quid ibi aliud dicemus, nisi «Deus meus es tu,» et «confitebor tibi; Deus meus es tu, et exaltabo te?» (Ps. CXVII, 28.) Non strepitu verborum istud dicemus, sed dilectio inhaerens illi, per se ipsam clamat istam vocem: Dilectio ipsa vox est. Haec de sublimi altare Dei in conspectu divinae majestatis ejus necessario in hoc loco ex sanctorum Patrum verbis posita sunt, ne quis carnaliter cogitans, aestimet in coelis esse altare corporeum, ex coelesti sive supercoelesti corpore factum; sed potius, juxta sensum spiritalium Patrum, intelligamus sublime altare Dei, rationabile et intelligibile esse in electa et rationali creatura, angelica videlicet et humana, quae in sanctis angelis, ex quo condita est, in sui contemplatione Conditoris sublimata, et sibi nimium per spiritum pacis unita, verum et sublime altare Dei existit, ex quo accipit Deus sempiternum sacrificium laudis et hostiam jubilationis, ad cujus altaris unitatem adjungitur nunc per fidem, et in futuro per divinae contemplationis speciem omnis multitudo hominum electorum.
chunks.english: Again, in another place, the same teacher explains the same verse that blessed Gregory explained. He says: “In that eternal house there is a sacrifice of praise; there is an eternal priest; and there is an eternal altar: the peaceful mind of the just. So it is not enough that on earth there should be that solemn day on which the Lamb was slain. Establish it as eternal in dense assemblies, searching out the high and hidden things, until, with your minds lifted up by God, you reach all the way to his divinity. And what will we do there except sing praises? What else will we say there except, ‘You are my God,’ and, ‘I will confess you; you are my God, and I will exalt you,’ Psalm one hundred seventeen, verse twenty-eight? We will not say this with the noise of words. Rather, love clinging to him cries out this voice by itself. Love itself is the voice.” These statements about the altar of God on high in the sight of his divine majesty had to be placed here from the words of the holy Fathers, so that no one, thinking in a fleshly way, should imagine that there is a bodily altar in heaven, made out of some heavenly or super-heavenly material. Instead, following the understanding of the spiritual Fathers, we should understand the altar of God on high to be rational and intelligible, existing in the chosen rational creature—that is, in angels and in human beings. In the holy angels, from the moment that creature was made, it has been lifted up in contemplation of its Creator and most closely united to itself through the spirit of peace. Thus it is the true and exalted altar of God, from which God receives the eternal sacrifice of praise and the offering of jubilation. To the unity of that altar is now joined, through faith, the whole multitude of elect human beings; and in the future they will be joined to it through the direct vision of divine contemplation.
chunks.notes: “in condensis” is rendered as “in dense assemblies,” preserving the printed sense; the phrase is unusual in this context. The Latin “rationabile et intelligibile” is rendered “rational and intelligible,” meaning a spiritual, intellectual reality rather than a material structure.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Sed quandiu in ista mortalitate vivunt, antequam reipsa ingrediantur ad illud altare Dei, antequam perveniant usque ad cornu altaris in orationibus et supplicationibus suis, tanquam in inferioribus adhuc positi, a supernis virtutibus juvantur, ut earum interventione exaudiantur, et quasi de sublimitate altaris suscipiantur; sicut legimus, et Danieli oranti et deprecanti Gabrielem angelum apparuisse, eique dixisse: «Ab initio precum tuarum egressus est sermo, et ego veni propter sermones tuos, et nemo est adjutor meus in omnibus nis, nisi Michael archangelus princeps vester» (Dan. IX, 23). Et in Zacharia propheta legimus pro consolatione et liberatione populi Dei angelum deprecantem et dicentem: «Domine exercituum, usquequo tu non misereberis Jerusalem et urbium Juda, quibus iratus es? Iste jam septuagesimus annus est» (Zach. II, 12). Et respondit Dominus angelo verba bona, verba consolatoria. Similiter et ad Tobiam Raphael angelus dicit: «Quando orabas tu cum lacrymis, et sepeliebas mortuos, ego obtuli orationem tuam Domino, et nunc misit me Dominus ut curarem te,» etc. (Tob. XII, 12). Fit ergo et in ista oratione et oblatione sacra consecrationis aliquid incomprehensibile et ineffabile, et multo his omnibus mirabilius, ut per angelica ministeria et supplicationes tanquam de sublimi altari divinae majestatis conspectibus offerantur in illa immolationis hora, cum astantibus sibi ministris coelestibus Christus, ut proposita consecret, adesse credendus est; de qua re commodum videtur aliqua beati Ambrosii verba ponere de Expositione Evangelii secundum Lucam (lib. I, n. 28): Non enim dubites, inquit, assistere angelum, quando Christus assistit, Christus immolatur. Etenim pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus; unde non immerito etiam Zachariae deprecanti apparuit angelus a dextris altaris incensi, quia veri sacerdotis jam nuntiabatur adventus et coeleste sacrificium parabatur, in quo angeli ministrarent. Sic ergo cogitanda sunt, ut aliquid quo nihil sit melius atque sublimius illa cogitatione conemur attingere.
chunks.english: But as long as the elect live in this mortal condition, before they actually enter that altar of God, and before they reach the horn of the altar in their prayers and supplications, they are still, as it were, down below. So they are helped by the powers above, in order that through their intercession they may be heard and, so to speak, received from the height of the altar. Thus we read that, when Daniel was praying and pleading, the angel Gabriel appeared to him and said: “From the beginning of your prayers the word went out, and I have come because of your words; and there is no one who helps me in all these things except Michael the archangel, your prince,” the book of Daniel, chapter nine, verse twenty-three. And in the prophet Zechariah we read that, for the consolation and liberation of God’s people, an angel prayed and said: “Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is now the seventieth year,” the book of Zechariah, chapter two, verse twelve. And the Lord answered the angel with good words, words of consolation. Likewise, the angel Raphael says to Tobias: “When you prayed with tears, and buried the dead, I offered your prayer to the Lord; and now the Lord has sent me to heal you,” and so on, the book of Tobit, chapter twelve, verse twelve. Therefore, in this prayer and offering of the sacred consecration, something incomprehensible and beyond speech takes place—something far more wonderful than all these examples: through angelic ministries and supplications, the offerings are presented, as if from the altar on high, before the sight of the divine majesty at that hour of sacrifice. For at that hour Christ must be believed to be present, with his heavenly ministers standing by him, so that he may consecrate the gifts set before him. On this point it seems useful to quote some words of blessed Ambrose from his Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke: “Do not doubt that an angel is present when Christ is present, when Christ is sacrificed. For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. And so it was not without reason that an angel appeared to Zechariah as he prayed, at the right side of the altar of incense: the coming of the true priest was already being announced, and the heavenly sacrifice was being prepared, in which the angels would minister.” So we should think about these things in such a way that, by that very thought, we try to reach something than which nothing is better or higher.
chunks.notes: The printed Latin has “in omnibus nis,” evidently corrupt; translated as “in all these things,” reading “his” or an equivalent sense. The Daniel citation is spoken as printed: “the book of Daniel, chapter nine, verse twenty-three,” although part of the quoted material corresponds more closely to Daniel chapter ten, verse twenty-one. The Zechariah citation is spoken as printed: “the book of Zechariah, chapter two, verse twelve,” though the quoted wording corresponds to Zechariah chapter one, verse twelve in common Vulgate numbering. “etc.” in the Tobit quotation is rendered “and so on.” The parenthetical Ambrose reference “(lib. I, n. 28)” is not a Scripture citation and is not spoken as such.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 67. Similiter quoque et illud quod sequitur: «Ut omnes, quotquot ex hac altaris participatione sacrosanctum Filii corpus et sanguinem sumpserimus, omni benedictione coelesti et gratia repleamur.» Ista enim munera, ista sunt dona super omnem gloriam constituta, quibus fideles suos omnipotens Deus reficiens, glorioso Filii sui corpore vivificat, sanctificat, aeternitati praeparat, per haec corda fidelium omni benedictione replet coelesti et gratia, tribuens corporibus castimoniam, mentibus fidem, cogitationibus puritatem. Per haec tuetur suos misericordia, confirmat spe, munit charitate, ut, tanta Domini participatione, intra se Deum suscipientes, templum ejus effici mereantur.
chunks.english: The same applies to what follows: “So that all of us, as many as receive from this sharing in the altar the most holy body and blood of the Son, may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace.” These are the gifts, these are the offerings, set above every glory. By them almighty God refreshes his faithful people; by the glorious body of his Son he gives them life, sanctifies them, and prepares them for eternity. Through these gifts he fills the hearts of the faithful with every heavenly blessing and grace, giving chastity to their bodies, faith to their minds, and purity to their thoughts. Through these gifts he protects his own with mercy, strengthens them with hope, and fortifies them with love, so that, by so great a sharing in the Lord and receiving God within themselves, they may deserve to become his temple.
chunks.notes: The quoted liturgical text is rendered according to the owner’s standardization for the Roman Canon while preserving Florus’s wording.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Quid sit ergo per participationem corporis et sanguinis Filii Dei omni benedictione coelesti et gratia repleri, et quantum hoc bonum debeat esuriri ac sitiri, audiamus beatum Ambrosium dulciter docentem et exhortantem: «Christus Ecclesiae cibus, Christus est potus. Caro Dei cibus, et Dei sanguis est potus. Christus nobis quotidie ministratur. Cibus iste non corpus impinguat, sed confirmat cor hominis. Hic est panis vitae: qui ergo vitam manducat mori non potest. Accedite ad eum, et satiamini, quia panis est. Accedite ad eum, et potate, quia fons est. Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini, quia lux est. Accedite ad eum et liberamini, quia ubi Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas. Accedite ad eum, et absolvemini, quia remissio peccatorum est. Corpus Domini Jesu postulatio est divinae reconciliationis et protectionis aeternae. Accipe tibi munimentum, suscipe Dominum Jesum tuae mentis hospitio: ubi corpus ejus, ibi Jesus est. Cum hospitium tuum adversarius viderit occupatum, coelestis fulgore prudentiae intelliget locum testamentis suis interclusum esse per Christum. Qui sit iste quaeris? Audi ipsum dicentem: «Ego sum panis vitae, qui venit ad me non esuriet; et qui credit in me non sitiet unquam» (Joan. VI, 35).» Sequitur in mysterio.
chunks.english: So what does it mean to be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace through sharing in the body and blood of the Son of God? And how greatly should we hunger and thirst for this good? Let us listen to blessed Ambrose, who teaches and exhorts us so sweetly: “Christ is the food of the Church; Christ is its drink. The flesh of God is food, and the blood of God is drink. Christ is ministered to us every day. This food does not fatten the body; it strengthens the human heart. This is the bread of life. Therefore, the one who eats life cannot die. Come to him and be satisfied, because he is bread. Come to him and drink, because he is a spring. Come to him and be enlightened, because he is light. Come to him and be set free, because where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. Come to him and be absolved, because he is the forgiveness of sins. The body of the Lord Jesus is the plea for divine reconciliation and eternal protection. Take this defense for yourself. Receive the Lord Jesus as the guest of your mind. Where his body is, there Jesus is. When the adversary sees that your guest-room is occupied, he will understand, by the brightness of heavenly wisdom, that through Christ the place is closed to his temptations. Do you ask who this is? Listen to him saying: ‘I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not hunger; and whoever believes in me will never thirst,’ the Gospel of John, chapter six, verse thirty-five.” The mystery continues.
chunks.notes: Printed “testamentis suis” is an evident misprint for “tentamentis suis” and is translated “his temptations”: the enemy finds no place for his assaults in the soul occupied by Christ.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 68. «Memento etiam, Domine, famulorum famularumque tuarum, qui nos praecesserunt cum signo fidei,» etc., usque «lucis et pacis indulgeas deprecamur.» Orat pia mater Ecclesia etiam pro defunctis suis, et eos sacrae oblationis intercessione commendat, certissime credens quia sanguis ille pretiosus, qui pro multis effusus est in remissionem peccatorum, non solum ad salutem viventium, sed etiam ad absolutionem valeat defunctorum, sicut beatus Joannes [Col. 0061B] testatur dicens: «Et sanguis Filii ejus Jesu Christi emundat nos ab omni peccato» (II Joan. I, 7). Procedunt enim fideles de corpore exeuntes ad Dominum, sed non praeceduntur ab Ecclesia, quia praecedunt cum signo fidei et dormiunt in somno pacis: cum signo fidei, quia ex aqua et Spiritu sancto renati, quia Christi cruce et passione signati. Dormiunt autem tanquam vere in resurrectione suscitandi, sicut Dominus de puella quam suscitaturus erat ait: «Non est mortua puella, sed dormit;» et de Lazaro: «Lazarus amicus noster dormit, sed vado ut a somno exsuscitem eum.» Unde et Apostolus de fidelibus defunctis ait: «Nolumus vos ignorare, fratres, de dormientibus, ut non contristemini, sicut et caeteri qui spem non habent.» Dormiunt ergo in somno pacis, quia ab unitate et societate Christi et Ecclesiae, nec per haereses, nec per schismata, nec per mortalia crimina separati sunt: in quibus etsi aliquando fuerunt, tamen per poenitentiam sanati, et per orationem Ecclesiae, cui in Petro dictum est: «Quodcunque solveritis super terram, erit solutum et in coelis,» reconciliati, (AUG.) et redemptionis mysterio sociati, utique in pace obierunt, miserante illo, qui non vult [Col. 0061C] mortem peccatoris, sed ut convertatur et vivat. Neque enim piorum animae mortuorum separantur ab Ecclesia, alioquin nec ad altare fieret eorum memoria in commemoratione corporis Christi, nec aliquid prodesset, ad ejus baptismum in periculis currere, ne sine illo finiatur in hac vita; nec ad reconciliationem, si forte per pravam vel malam conscientiam quisque ab eodem corpore separatus est. Cur enim ista fiunt, nisi quia fideles etiam defuncti membra sunt ejus? Quamvis ergo nondum cum suis corporibus, jam tamen animae regnant cum Christo. Unde et in Apocalypsi legitur: «Beati mortui qui in Domino moriuntur, amodo jam dicit Spiritus ut requiescant a laboribus suis, opera enim illorum sequuntur illos» (Apoc. XIV, 13); et ipse est verus sabbatismus [Col. 0061D] fidelium, id est requies, de qua dicit Apostolus: «Itaque relinquitur sabbatismus populo Dei» (Hebr. IV, 9). Qui enim ingressus est in requiem ejus, requievit ab operibus suis, quemadmodum et a suis Deus. Regnat itaque cum Christo nunc Ecclesia in vivis et mortuis. Propterea enim, sicut dicit Apostolus: «Mortuus est Christus, ut et vivorum et mortuorum dominetur» (Rom. XIV, 9). Unde et alibi ait: «Quoniam non posuit nos Deus ad iram, sed in acquisitionem salutis per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, qui mortuus est pro nobis, ut, sive vigilemus, sive dormiamus, cum illo vivamus» (I Thess. V, 9). In quibus verbis vigilantes, viventes, dormientes, mortuos intelligi voluit, sicut iterum dicit: «Sive»[Col. 0062A] «ergo vivamus, sive moriamur, Domini sumus» (Rom. XIV, 8).
chunks.english:
“Remember also, Lord, your servants, men and women, who have gone before us with the sign of faith,” and so on, as far as, “of light and peace, we pray that you grant.” The loving mother, the Church, also prays for her dead. She commends them through the intercession of the sacred offering, firmly believing that the precious blood poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins has power not only for the salvation of the living, but also for the absolution of the dead. As blessed John testifies: “And the blood of his Son Jesus Christ cleanses us from every sin,” John’s second letter, chapter one, verse seven.

For the faithful, when they leave the body, go forward to the Lord. Yet they are not cut off from the Church, because they have gone before us “with the sign of faith” and “sleep in the sleep of peace.” They go with the sign of faith because they have been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, and because they have been marked by Christ’s cross and passion. They sleep because they are truly to be awakened in the resurrection. So the Lord said of the girl whom he was about to raise: “The girl is not dead, but sleeping.” And of Lazarus he said: “Our friend Lazarus is sleeping; but I am going to awaken him from sleep.” Therefore the Apostle says about the faithful who have died: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, about those who are sleeping, so that you may not grieve like the others, who have no hope.”

So they sleep in the sleep of peace because they have not been separated from the unity and fellowship of Christ and the Church, either by heresies, or by schisms, or by deadly sins. And even if they were once caught in such things, they were healed by repentance and reconciled through the prayer of the Church, to whom it was said in Peter: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.” [Augustine] Joined to the mystery of redemption, they certainly died in peace, through the mercy of him who does not want the death of the sinner, but wants the sinner to turn back and live.

For the souls of the devout dead are not separated from the Church. Otherwise, their memorial would not be made at the altar in the commemoration of Christ’s body. Nor would it do any good to hurry to his baptism in times of danger, lest this life end without it; nor to hurry to reconciliation, if someone has been separated from that same body by a corrupt and evil conscience. Why are these things done, unless the faithful, even when dead, are still his members? So although their souls do not yet reign with Christ together with their bodies, still their souls already reign with him.

Hence we read in the Apocalypse: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From now on, the Spirit says that they may rest from their labors, for their works follow them,” the Book of Revelation, chapter fourteen, verse thirteen. This is the true sabbath-rest of the faithful—that is, their rest—about which the Apostle says: “And so there remains a sabbath-rest for the people of God,” the letter to the Hebrews, chapter four, verse nine. For whoever has entered his rest has rested from his own works, just as God did from his.

Therefore the Church now reigns with Christ in both the living and the dead. For this reason, as the Apostle says: “Christ died, so that he might be Lord of both the living and the dead,” Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter fourteen, verse nine. And elsewhere he says: “For God has not appointed us for wrath, but for obtaining salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that whether we are awake or asleep, we may live with him,” Paul’s first letter to the Thessalonians, chapter five, verse nine. By these words he intended “the awake” to mean the living, and “the sleeping” to mean the dead, just as he says again: “So whether we live or whether we die, we belong to the Lord,” Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter fourteen, verse eight.
chunks.notes: The printed citation “II Joan. I, 7” is rendered as printed, but the quotation is actually from John’s first letter, chapter one, verse seven. Source siglum rendered as [Augustine]: printed “(AUG.)”. Printed “sed non praeceduntur ab Ecclesia” (“they are not preceded by the Church”) is an evident misprint for “praeciduntur” and is translated “they are not cut off from the Church”.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 69. (GREG.) Nam luce clarius constat quia perfectorum justorum animae, mox ut hujus carnis claustra exeunt, in coelestibus sedibus recipiuntur, quod et ipsa Veritas attestatur dicens: «Ubi fuerit corpus, illic congregabuntur et aquilae» (Matth. XXIV, 28), quia ubi ipse Redemptor noster est corpore, illic procul dubio colligentur et animae justorum. Et Paulus dissolvi desiderat et cum Christo esse. Qui ergo Christum in coelo esse non dubitat, nec Pauli animam in coelo esse negat, qui etiam dissolutione sui corporis atque inhabitatione patriae coelestis dicit: «Scimus quoniam si terrestris domus nostra hujus habitationis dissolvatur, quod aedificationem habemus»[Col. 0062B] «ex Deo domum non manu factam aeternam in coelis» (II Cor. V, 5).
chunks.english:
[Gregory] It is clearer than daylight that the souls of the perfectly righteous, as soon as they leave the enclosure of this flesh, are received into the heavenly dwellings. Truth himself bears witness to this when he says: “Where the body is, there the eagles will gather,” the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-four, verse twenty-eight. For where our Redeemer himself is in body, there, without any doubt, the souls of the righteous will also be gathered.

And Paul longs to be dissolved and to be with Christ. So whoever does not doubt that Christ is in heaven must not deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven. For Paul also speaks of the dissolution of his body and of his dwelling in the heavenly homeland when he says: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens,” Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter five, verse five.
chunks.notes: Source siglum rendered as [Gregory]: printed “(GREG.)”. The printed citation “II Cor. V, 5” is rendered as printed, although the wording corresponds chiefly to Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter five, verse one.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 70. (VIGILIUS.) Verum hoc de apostolis, martyribus, confessoribus, caeterisque perfectioris vitae viris, ut jam diximus, fieri credendum est. Nam sunt quorumdam justorum animae, quae coelesti regno, licet in beata requie, quibusdam adhuc mansionibus differuntur, in quo dilationis damno quid aliud ostenditur nisi quod de perfecta justitia aliquid minus habuerunt. At vero nonnulli propter bona quidem fidei opera ad electorum sortem praeordinati, sed propter mala aliqua quibus polluti de corpore exierunt, post mortem severe castigandi excipiuntur flammis ignis purgatorii, et vel usque ad diem judicii longa examinatione a vitiorum sorde mundantur, vel certe prius amicorum fidelium precibus, eleemosynis, jejuniis, [Col. 0062C] fletibus et hostiae salutaris oblationibus, poenis absoluti, et ipsi ad beatorum perveniunt requiem. Illis ergo eorum sacrae victimae mortuis prosunt, qui hic vivendo obtinuerunt ut eos etiam post mortem bona adjuvent, quae hic pro ipsis ab aliis fiunt. Inter haec autem pensandum est, quod «tutior via sit,» ut bonum quod quisque post mortem sperat agi per alios, agat dum vivit ipse pro se. Beatius quippe est liberum exire quam post vincula libertatem quaerere. Post illa ergo verba quibus dicitur, «qui nos praecesserunt cum signo fidei, et dormiunt in somno pacis,» usus fuit antiquorum, sicut etiam Romana agit Ecclesia, ut statim recitarentur ex diptychis, id est tabulis, nomina defunctorum, atque ita post lectionem nominum subjungerentur verba sequentia: «Ipsis et»[Col. 0062D] «omnibus in Christo quiescentibus locum refrigerii, lucis et pacis ut indulgeas deprecamur.» Ipsis videlicet quorum nomina memorantur, et caeteris omnibus in Christo quiescentibus, de quibus dicit Apostolus: «Et mortui qui in Christo sunt resurgent primi,» «locum refrigerii,» ubi non sentitur ille ardor poenarum, ubi dives ille in inferno sepultus dicebat: «Quia crucior in hac flamma.» «Et lucis,» quam Dominus promittit fidelibus, dicens: «Ego sum lux mundi; qui sequitur me non ambulabit in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitae;» et de qua Psalmista ait: «Ut placeam coram Deo in lumine viventium» (Psal. LV, 14). «Et pacis,» ad quam justus Simeon, finitis vitae hujus laboribus, transire cupiebat, dicens: «Nunc dimittis servum tuum, Domine, secundum verbum tuum in pace» (Luc. II, 29). Et in qua sanctorum martyrum animae quiescunt, dicente Scriptura: «Visi sunt oculis insipientium mori, illi autem sunt in pace» (Sap. III, 2, 3).
chunks.english:
[Vigilius] Yet this should be believed, as we have already said, about the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and the other men of more perfect life. For there are souls of certain righteous people who, although they are in blessed rest, are still delayed from the kingdom of heaven in certain dwelling places. In the harm caused by this delay, what else is shown except that they lacked something of perfect righteousness?

But some people, because of their good works of faith, have indeed been appointed beforehand to the lot of the elect. Yet because of certain evils by which they were stained when they left the body, after death they are received for severe correction into the flames of purifying fire. Either they are cleansed from the stain of their faults by a long testing up to the day of judgment, or else, before that day, they are released from their punishments through the prayers, alms, fasts, tears, and offerings of the saving Victim made by their faithful friends. Then they too reach the rest of the blessed.

So the sacred sacrificial offerings benefit those dead persons who, while living here, gained the grace that after death they would be helped by the good works done for them here by others. But in all this we must consider that “the safer path” is this: whatever good a person hopes others will do for him after death, he should do for himself while he is alive. For it is more blessed to go out free than to seek freedom after being bound.

After the words, “who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace,” the custom of the ancients was—and the Roman Church still acts this way—that the names of the dead were immediately read from the diptychs, that is, from the tablets. And after the reading of the names, these following words were added: “For these, and for all who rest in Christ, we pray that you grant them a place of refreshment, light, and peace.” That means: for those whose names are remembered, and for all the others who rest in Christ, about whom the Apostle says, “And the dead who are in Christ will rise first.”

“A place of refreshment”: where the burning heat of punishments is not felt, the heat of which the rich man buried in hell spoke when he said, “For I am tormented in this flame.” “And of light”: the light the Lord promises to the faithful when he says, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” The Psalmist also speaks of it: “That I may be pleasing before God in the light of the living,” the Psalms, Psalm fifty-five, verse fourteen. “And of peace”: the peace into which righteous Simeon desired to pass when the labors of this life were finished, saying, “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace,” the Gospel of Luke, chapter two, verse twenty-nine. And it is the peace in which the souls of the holy martyrs rest, as Scripture says: “In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to die, but they are in peace,” the Wisdom of Solomon, chapter three, verses two through three.
chunks.notes: Source siglum rendered as [Vigilius]: printed “(VIGILIUS.)”. The printed citation “Psal. LV, 14” is rendered as printed; numbering and verse division may differ in modern Bibles, and the wording echoes Psalm fifty-six in some enumerations. The liturgical phrase is abbreviated and paraphrased only to the extent present in the Latin.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 71. Hanc autem piam et religiosam observantiam, quam ex apostolica sine dubio traditione susceptam [Col. 0063A] universa in mundo uniformiter et celebriter tenet Ecclesia, etiam Veteris Testamenti Scriptura et consuetudo a Patribus custodita diligentissime commendat. Legimus namque in Machabaeorum libris, quod vir fortissimus et pontifex Judas, duodecim millia drachmas argenti misit Jerosolymam offerri pro peccatis mortuorum qui in bello ceciderant, considerans quod hi qui cum pietate dormitionem acceperant, optimam haberent repositam gratiam; ubi et hoc in laudibus fidei ejus adjungitur, quia et sancta et salubri cogitatione pro defunctis exorabat, ut a peccato solverentur. Sequitur in mysterio:
chunks.english:
This devout and religious practice, which the whole Church throughout the world holds uniformly and solemnly—having without doubt received it from apostolic tradition—is also very carefully commended by the Scripture of the Old Testament and by the custom preserved by the Fathers. For we read in the books of the Maccabees that the most courageous man and high priest Judas sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem to be offered for the sins of the dead who had fallen in battle. He considered that those who had accepted their death in godliness had a most excellent grace stored up for them. And in praise of his faith, this too is added: that with holy and saving thought he prayed for the dead, so that they might be released from sin.

The mystery continues:
chunks.notes: The passage alludes to the second book of Maccabees, chapter twelve, but no exact citation is printed in the Latin, so none has been added in the narration. Florus calls Judas “pontifex”, translated “high priest” as he wrote it; historically Judas Maccabeus did not hold the high priesthood.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 72. «Nobis quoque peccatoribus famulis tuis,» etc., usque «Per Christum Dominum nostrum.» Commendatio pro spiritibus defunctorum per oblationem pietatis, [Col. 0063B] ut in beatis electorum sedibus mereantur obtinere locum refrigerii, lucis et pacis. Consequenter oratur omnipotens Deus ut etiam caeteros fideles, qui superstites sunt et vivunt, id est sacerdotes et populum, per virtutem et gratiam ejus Deus venerabilis sacramenti auxilio ad eamdem beatitudinem perducat. Totius namque Ecclesiae vox est, id est sacerdotum et plebium cum humilitate et contritione cordis dicentium Deo: «Nobis quoque peccatoribus famulis tuis:» quia, licet omni tempore peccatores nos esse ex corde cognoscere debeamus, tamen maxime hoc attentius agendum et confitendum est, cum in illo sacro mysterio celebratur remissionis gratia, indulgentia peccatorum, et cum humilitate et contritione cordis dicendum Deo: «Nobis quoque peccatoribus»[Col. 0063C] «famulis tuis,» quia, sicut scriptum est, etsi peccaverimus, tui sumus, scientes magnitudinem tuam, non de ullis nostris meritis, sed «de multitudine miserationum tuarum sperantibus,» corde in psalmo cantamus: «Et secundum multitudinem miserationum tuarum dele iniquitatem meam» (Psal. L, 3). Recordanda namque sunt in hoc loco, et diligenter inculcanda verba Apostoli, dicentis: «Omnis namque sacerdos ex hominibus assumptus, pro hominibus constituitur in his quae sunt ad Deum, ut offerat dona et sacrificia pro peccatis: qui condolere possit his qui ignorant et errant, quoniam et ipse circumdatus est infirmitate, et propterea debet, quemadmodum pro populo, ita etiam pro se offerre pro peccatis» (Hebr. V, 1). Ad quod beatus Gregorius in quodam loco exhortans [Col. 0063D] dicit: «Sed necesse est ut, cum haec agimus, nosmetipsos Deo in cordis contritione mactemus; quia qui passionis Dominicae mysteria celebramus, debemus imitari quod agimus. Tunc enim vere pro nobis Deo hostia erit, cum nos ipsos hostiam fecerit. Oratur itaque omnipotens Deus, ut non solum defunctis, quorum supra commemoratio facta est, sed etiam nobis peccatoribus, de multitudine miserationum suarum sperantibus, partem aliquam et societatem donare dignetur cum suis sanctis apostolis et martyribus et omnibus sanctis, ut pro modulo nostro, quibus nunc sociamur per communionem fidei, quorum memoriam veneramur, in quorum communione et unitate haec divina mysteria agimus, cum ipsis etiam societatem vitae et beatitudinis aeternae in futuro accipiamus. Intra quorum nos consortium ut [Col. 0064A] nos Dei pietas introducat petimus; ut nobis non nostri meriti aestimator, sed veniae sit largitor; ut, quia sanctorum societati per meritum jungi non possumus, per indulgentiam conjungamur. Si enim aestimemur, et divino judicio ponderemur, nullus ad apostolorum et martyrum societatem assurget. In fine autem hujus orationis, sicut et in caeteris praecedentibus subjungitur «Per Christum Dominum nostrum,» et statim conclusio totius consecrationis sequitur dicendo:
chunks.english:
“To us sinners also, your servants,” and so on, as far as “Through Christ our Lord.” This is a commendation of the spirits of the dead through the offering of mercy, so that, among the blessed dwellings of the elect, they may be worthy to receive a place of refreshment, light, and peace. Next, almighty God is prayed to bring the rest of the faithful as well—the ones who still remain alive, that is, the priests and the people—to that same blessedness, by his power and grace, and with the help of the venerable sacrament.
